One of the things that always goes unanswered revolves around "computers for agents". The "agent" isn't an entity, doesn't hold any wealth, and can't buy anything. So the expectation is people or businesses buying these computers at tens of thousands of dollars each to run AI models. The thing though, is anyone who has ever tried to get a business they work for to buy new pc hardware, or even upgrade to an ssd over an hdd (this was a fight even 6 years ago), is like pulling teeth. Instead of buying 150 new $800 desktops the expectation is now for them to buy 150 $10,000 desktops and host a local server to run a bunch of agents. No company is going to do this at scale. 

Most companies outside of the tech industry haven't seen large growth like is reflected by the stock market overall, so asking for millions of investments for something that to this day has no positive return or workflow improvement is beyond insane. Everyone gets it, this is a bubble, but at some point all that investor money is going to need a positive ROI or else the power bill won't be paid and the AI datacenter will be a large outdated concrete slab covered in fancy sand.

Yes, please! Premium segment isn't a bad idea and in my opinion be quiet! is well positioned to create the ultimate mATX solution of (airflow and silence focused) mATX case + SFX or SFX-L PSU + CPU cooler/s.

Incidentally I had an ID-Cooling Frostflow AIO cooler on my older PC, and replaced it middle of last year with a Thermalright Assassin Spirit 120 v2. The ID Cooling was still working, but I installed it in early 2017, so it was already 8+ years in operation. I thought it was time to replace it, even if no signs to do so, it could become a problem sooner or later just because of age and wear. Replacing it with the Assassin showed in fact better thermals for my CPU (an Intel i7-6700K) right away. So yes, the AIO was working fine, but after that many years, and two-three thermal paste replacements, the cheapest Assassin aircooler was in fact a better cooler. After the swap, I also noticed that the Id Cooling fans had become slightly noisy, the Assassin in comparison is quieter. Well it's also one instead of two fans of course. But in any case, thanks ID Cooling for a super reliable and trusty AIO cooler that did it's job fine and then some all these years. Had I known of this $18 air cooler of yours, I would have gone for it to replace the Frostflow. This older PC is now a Fedora PC running  two VMs: a pfSense firewall, and a TrueNAS little server (2x 12 TB WD Red plus HDDs in a mirror). As old as it is, this computer is quite the reliable workhorse in my home lab, and basically it has become my main home server. An air cooler in it brings some extra peace of mind knowing there won't be any leak risks in it.

I like how he points out the ribs and other punching/embossing to add strength to a thin piece of sheet metal. It's common practice in building lightweight frames and panels in building cars that I've been doing for 20 years that I also brought into my own custom fabricated cases in my workshop (along with dimples/circle cuts, which would be pressing/punching a circle out of the sheet, but leaving an embossed/raised edge while removing the circle of material, which both strengthens and lightens the panel or even frames depending on application). A lot of people think that it's just decorative or for a clearance maybe, but it is a key detail in strengthening, especially when dealing with sheets of this thickness.

In general that was another interesting conversation on manufacturing. I have degrees in Mathematics but came home and continued to work in my machine shop filled with tools/machinery that I inherited from the old master machinist that taught me growing up. It's fun to hear people talking about tooling and automation for modern lines, especially when they're trying to simplify the explanation. He did a good job trying to simplify the process while also dealing with a bit of a language barrier (that's definitely not your average conversation for a language that isn't your first, lol).

When it comes to 3D Printing,
The Choice of material and Printing Method is really key.
the most common type of printer is called an "FDM Printer" (Fused Deposition Modeling),
and it seems to be what was used for this video.

FDM machines are good Generalists because they allow you to print relatively large parts, at a decent speed in a large varriety of polymers.
the most common being PLA and PETG.
but there are other materials worth looking at such as:
- PBT (Similar in Print characteristics to PLA, but all arround better in it's mechanical properties.)
- ABS (which you may know from keyboards and the like) 
- ASA (an ABS derivative for easier printing)
- PCTG (an imporved version of PETG with better mechanical and printing properties)
- PET (like PETG without the softener, making it much stiffer in mechanical applications. CF filler is reccomended due to it's better printing characteristics)
- Nylons (PA-6 and PA-12 being the most common, but they are really hard to work with glass-fiber filler "PA-GF" makes it much easier to work while retaining good mechanical properties.)
- PEEK ( A Super-Polymer, Amazing mechanical properties but it requires a really well tuned machien to work with, and each spool is extremely expensive)
- PEKK is a cheaper but much more workable version of PEEK, using the same Polymers just in a diffrent ratio.
A lot of the ones listed here require special parts, (direct drives, Hardend nozzles, heated-enclosures)
Fillers such as CF and GF and give stiffness, and sometimes improve printing behavior by countering effects like warping.

but there are also some other methods for printing such as 
- SLA (Stereolithography) / resin printing 
- SLS (Selective Laser Sintering) / Power Printing

SLA is great for extreme detail and dimensional accuracy but it has a more limited selection of materials.
Most SLA systems are built for mainly high-resoloution Decorative models such as rings and miniatures,
and the material provided for this kind of work often does not state the exact polymers used, instead they just provide a spec-sheet with its mechanical properties.
However, there are Engnieering Grade machines that can print well-known polymers such as:
- Nylon (11/12) in (normal, CF and GF)
- ABS composites
- PP
- HDT
- PEEK
- POM/Delrin

SLS Printers are actually used in the industry for Engnieering and prototyping Work,
but they are very expensive to purchase and maintain.
due to them using power, you never need to print support, so you can make a lot of shapes you couldnt on any other type of machine.
The most common material here is PA-6 or PA-12 and its composites (PA-CF)

I know the pain of a house fire. I've survived two of them... The first in an apartment building where the apartment DIRECTLY above mine caught fire. Much of my property was lost not due to fire, but due to the water and whatever the fire department added to it that seeped through the floor of the apartment above and through my ceiling. In the boundless infinite wisdom of the dwellers above, they left a candle burning when they left for the day. They lost everything in the fire itself, I lost most of my belongings to the black water that gushed through my ceiling and walls. Yay.

The 2nd time was at my parent's house. I moved back in with them because they needed assistance and I needed space to work on my bus conversion (motorhome/motorcoach) and I had soooo many computers. Including a populated half-rack enclosure, my split power backup (the battery part weighed close to 300 pounds!) The fire swept through half the house VERY quickly. The bus was parked right up to the eves of the house so it'd fit in the driveway. 

Unfortunately, the fire started in the garage. Everything I had bought over a period of two years or so was inside the garage. Including 20# and 30# propane canisters for various things including for the BBQ grill in the back yard.

The bus went quick. That and the things I had in the garage were worth around $200,000 along with an estimated $50k in computers, servers, battery backup units, line conditioners, etc...

It took me a couple of decades to (mostly) recover from those fires. Sigh. Not counting the server I'm renting, I now have just two servers, both in one of those dual-split modular server cases. No rack anymore, but I wish I still had the one I had. That thing was AWESOME. I recovered it from a store that closed. It was originally on adjustable feet for leveling it. I took those off and put these HUGE casters on it. I could unplug it from the battery backup system and the LAN and just wheel it around if I needed to.  

Ah well... I can't take anything with me into the abyssal oblivion of death anyway. Those two fires cured me of being materialistic. Most of my spending now are limited primarily to computers and electronics that I can tinker with rather than jewelry or sports cars or artworks or... Well, anything outside of computers and electronics! Outside of that, I buy what I NEED for the most part. Though, I will admit... I did get one of those "buttons" you can program with pictures or looped video clips. I got that to see if the image quality was REALLY what it appeared to be in the product photo... I was VERY pleasantly surprised when it arrived... The quality was ACTUALLY that good! Now I might have to get another to rip apart and see if I can use it in a RPi or Arduino device. It even has touch screen! 

Anyway, this comment has gotten out of hand. I think I'll finish it right here. 😂

I use OpenFOAM in my daily work, and I feel like this makes sense - OpenFOAM is programmed quite similarly to a game, because it's a very modular framework with a lot of OOP related overhead due to virtual function calls and so, so cache matters a lot. But in contrast to a game, it will happily run on all 16 cores of the CPU. This means that there's actually an uplift by getting that second CCD of higher cache cores vs a game which, if i understand this correctly, is just moved to fit on the cores on the high cache CCD, so if it uses less than 8 cores, the additional high cache CCD is pretty much useless.

AMD also made ECC memory support worse. Ryzen 9000 officially supports DDR5-5600 on AM5 and that completely worked fine with DDR5-5600 ECC UDIMMs for years. With the recent AGESA 1.3.0.0 AMD decided to lock ECC memory at DDR5-5200, you cannot even select a slower frequency.

Up until now it had been the practice that the BIOS loaded the default JEDEC frequency and timings but you were free to manually change those settings at your own risk.

Overclocking ECC memory for example is useful to verify how the system reacts when memory errors occur and that those errors are properly logged.

I had two 3870s in crossfire that could run Crysis pretty well at high settings. My friend had a 4870. ATI made some great hardware back then, starting with the legendary 9700 Pro/9800 Pro cards. A part of me wishes I could go back to the era. Being hyped and excited for any bit of news and tidbits regarding Half Life 2, Doom 3, FEAR, and Crysis is something I'll never forget.

This is absolutely the kind of video I would like to see more of, especially in a time when people are returning to older hardware and games more than ever. I love learning and talking about computer hardware of years passed, especially when there is interesting historical context behind it. My favorite period of PC gaming hardware is 2003-2005, right on the edge where PCIe gradually replaced AGP while hardware improved by leaps and bounds. I've always been curious how the AGP versions of high-end cards (like the GeForce 7800) stacked up against their PCIe counterparts, but I've never owned the right cards to test that.
In regard to the point of the card's thermal design, I think it's important to remember that high airflow was still a relatively new idea back in these days. Plenty of people were still using cases with just a couple of 80mm fans at the back and hardly any intake vents at the front. The blower design would be compensating for this, ensuring the GPU isn't reliant upon the case's airflow design for its own ability to remove heat from the case. 
In the case of this GPU not working, I'm not sure just how many configurations you tried, but I've always struggled getting GPUs older than Radeon HD 5000 to work on UEFI boards of any age. An AM2+ or LGA1366 system with a traditional BIOS would probably give you the best chance of hardware compatibility. Additionally, I would stay away from nForce chipsets, because their reliability has become questionable in their old age. It probably just doesn't work correctly, though, being an engineering sample.

Steve, you call these CPU's reminiscent of the first generation Ryzen CPU's and to some extend I agree (compared to the previous Intel CPU's it does seem a step in the right direction). But in terms performance and certainly power usage is more reminiscent of the older AMD FX (8350, 8370) CPU's: decent or good productivity performance, quite a ways behind in gaming (the 270K Plus often does not even beat the 2 generations old 5xxx X3D parts) and still way too high power usage. And these CPU's are also priced like the AMD FX CPU's back then; quite reasonable and lower then you might expect.

All in all these Intel seems to be getting their act back together. I am not surprised that this swing might take several generations and multiple years to accomplish, if you know about how chips are designed and made. And by that I mean how the actual chips are designed and produced in the ASML provided EUV machines and the whole chain around it; it can take months to the better part of a year for a chip to go from a plan/blueprint to fully working. So if it doesn't work as expected (i.e. an architecture not turning out how you wanted it to be),  you could be months and months along. And it's not that you make a hand full of chips, go through that whole process, evaluate it and if it sucks redesign and try again... then you're without a new generation of chips for 3-5 years. There will be some experimental testing, but at an early point you have to call it good enough and just start mass producing the CPU's and hope you can do some stuff in microcode. And then, if they turn out "meh", rather try again in a year with a refresh.

A point of clarification on Element's "voice rooms": There is a beta feature called Video Rooms that you have to enable under Settings > Labs. This gets you a similar experience to discords voice channels, it works on mobile, supports screen sharing and video, and runs on matrix itself. The Jitsi integration that was mentioned was an old integration with Jitsi (a similar product to zoom) that would basically put a widget for Jitsi in your channel. It was always kinda janky and has been basically replaced with the new beta voice room feature. Also, because the new voice rooms are part of the matrix protocol, other clients should be adding support if they haven't already. It looks like Commet might support it already as an example

Something really cool I've found with the Matrix protocol is its federation, meaning you can chat with people from different self-hosted instances, while non-federated platforms limit you to whoever's on the same instance.

I worked in the marketing department at Antec during the release of the NINE HUNDRED. Great to see there are still fans of that case and that people remember it. Definitely my favorite product from when I worked there. Part of my job was writing box and ad copy; so, I actually wrote the ridiculous box copy that you highlighted (good times!). I was deep into the local LAN party scene at the time. In fact, the first time the case was shown to the public was at Showdown LAN 2006 in San Jose. We showed early production samples at the event because it was just before the product launch. My boss gave me one of the samples and I built a system into it using a Danger Den water-cooling kit that I got at the LAN. So, my Nine Hundred is the first one to ever have a water-cooled system built into it (yes, I still have it). Also, I looked through my old notes and found some copy I wrote for a Nine Hundred Fan naming contest. Apparently the idea was to solicit names from the public for the 200mm fan. I don't recall if we ever did it, or if "Big Boy" was something the head of the marketing department came up with.

It's worth noting that the City of London is not London, it's the ancient part of London dating back to its founding, and it functions separately from the rest of London. This includes having its own government and police force, the City of London Police.
These days the City of London is the business district of London, focusing on Banking/Insurance/Law - and is also known as "The Square Mile". (Guess how big it is? Yeah.)
There are around 15,000 residents in the City, but the population grows to around 350,000 each weekday with commuters. The City of London police has over 800 officers to police those residents and commuters, and to quote some ex-officers  I know from another force they "are great at parades and ceremonies, but couldn't catch a cold". The police force for the other 10 million residents of London is the Metropolitan Police, who aren't perfect, but are too big to get away with this kind of crap.
Post 2000 the City of London Police decided to do a lot more IP work, and have a history of "working closely" with IP holders - there are previous "irregularities" with their work with other IP owners. Searching Techdirt for them is a good starting point. This behaviour is not unusual or unexpected. Other police forces are larger, have more oversight, and that'll be why IP owners don't want them to do this work.

As a Chinese, I’ve visited Shenzhen and many other Tier-1 and Tier-2 cities, and what stood out to me was how differently “repair” is defined there.

In China, repair work naturally falls into three tiers.
Tier 1 is an individual with screwdrivers and basic tools—simple diagnostics, part swaps, the kind of work most people in the West would recognize as “repair.”
Tier 2 involves technicians with microscopes, soldering stations, and programming tools, capable of board-level repair and component replacement.
Tier 3 goes even further: technicians with virtually every tool imaginable, able to revive devices that would be considered beyond saving elsewhere—everything short of fabricating the chip itself.

In contrast, much of the Western world treats repair as a labor-cost problem. High wages make deep repair economically irrational, so “repair” often just means replacing entire modules or assemblies.

TLDR: This is how you do it right.
1. Cap your FPS so it is always below capping your GPU. Maybe 80-90% and below. Try and not cap below 40FPS and definitely not below 30. 50-60 will feel very nice. 40 is acceptable. 
2. Set frame gen between 2-4x to hit fps and acceptable response feel.
3. If 2 isnt hitting your FPS, set the SCALING FACTOR to 1.05 to 1.2 (this reduces rendering resolution the higher you go)

For example, im Minecraft with shaders on at 4K im sitting at 100% GPU use at 55-60fps. I reduce this to cap to 50fps and my GPU sits around 70-90%. I then turn on 2x frame gen, grab 100fps CONSTANT and continue to sit at 70-90% never capping the GPU. CONSISTANT FPS is amazing to have and my tradeoff was maybe 30% higher latency that I cannot even feel. (i do start to feel it at 4x). I can even do a baseline of 40fps and get 80FPS consistantly and be around 50-60% GPU useage. at 4k WITH shaders. Over time this SAVES ME MONEY in my electric bill. Over a year I will have likely made up the cost of the utility. This is invaluable to me. I can do this in any game now, and if a game is especially bad to get a 40fps+ baseline to work from, I use scaling to reduce the render resolution slightly. It is very hard to tell a render resolution of 1.1 from 1.0 but it is VERY easy to see the jump in the baseline FPS that has a huge impact on framegen multipliers and latency later. The tool is just so good as a gamer.

This is a very powerful utility that i wish I was smart enough to have programmed myself because every gamer should own it.

In my own little testing, I found that Lossless Upscaling is especially useful on the Steam Deck where the much smaller screen resolution is easier to upscale resulting in overall acceptable latency increases and visual artifacts are much harder to spot and easier to live with.
A noticeable exception is Indiana Jones where the latency increase was to high that even though the result is still playable, the artifacts and latency are borderline in some cases. The GPU is simply maxed out in that game and scaling doesn't make it much better.
A good example is Diablo 2 Resurrected: without lossless scaling I get about 48fps in the fifth act in the city. Then, I cap it to 30FPS and start lossless scaling 2X to bring it up to 60FPS. This results in less power consumed and a much smoother, more consistent visuals! If you usually have FPS slightly over 30FPS consistently, then capping to 30FPS and adding 2X frame gen is the way to go. The LCD Deck can't go over 60fps anyways - a bit unfortunate but a reasonable improvement over anything lower than 60FPS.

The point about surface vs device temperatures at the end is very insightful; many devices that end up in a "handheld consumer-facing" use-case are often much more tightly constrained by strict limits on the surface skin temperatures than the actual limits of the parts themselves. This is obviously true for handheld consoles, but also things like tablets/laptops; the Surface Pro for example has sensors specifically to ensure the device casing doesn't exceed something around 40-45c, regardless of how hot/cool the actual processor is, and this is usually the limiting factor.

There are in fact small clip-on accessories some people have created to cool off a specific location on the outside of the device to allow it to run at full power longer without thermal throttling. If you're not _actually_ holding the unit in your hands, it doesn't really matter if the casing gets up to 50-60c, but you'll burn yourself right quick if you touch an aluminum or magnesium surface at that temperature so manufacturers can't sell a device like that.

42:59 The sensitivity thing he mentioned about the thumbsticks was kinda glossed over but it's incredibly important. Hall sticks have horrible sensitivity feel because of the inherent sensitivity curves they have, and most TMR still have that problem, just less so. The sticks they used do not have a response curve problem and are actually linear output, so they're a 1 to 1 replacement for Potentiometer sticks that also have can't get sensor drift. For context, this controller has more accurate sticks than the popular GameSir G7 Pro.

TLDR: I like this case! I moved my existing gaming rig from a Phanteks Evolv X into this one, and my CPU average temperature dropped from 36C to ~27C. That's HUGE. Practical impact is that the room doesn't heat up as quickly because the system doesn't have to work so hard to cool itself, which is also great on my electric bill. It's really easy to build in, has plenty of room to work in, and honestly has pretty solid build quality. The glass panel absolutely helps with the airflow getting to the CPU and GPU, so don't for a second think it's just gimmicky - even Steve points out in this video that the glass panel serves a solid function for cooling. 

If you're really concerned about noise, replace all your fans with low-dB fans. Aside from any AIO pumps, those make the most noise in any build.

I highly recommend this case. Been building PCs FOREVER and this one looks great, is really easy to work in, and has great airflow. Perfect for any gaming rig or just regular desktop computing use.

That's powder coating, not painting. Paint is a liquid product, usually water or solvent-based.  Powder coating is electro-statically charged powder that is then baked to cure. 

Also, the preheat before powdering also reduces off-gassing, a chemical reaction in most metals when they're heated. Aluminum is one of the worst offenders, and if not preheated before coating, it will produce micro bubbles in the finish.

As owner of a powder coat shop, I get very offended at calling it "paint". ;)

This takes me back.  I used to work on an SMT line on a Siemens D4 and D2.  Considering how fast and accurate the machines are they are pretty reliable.  The main maintenance problem we faced was poor part pickup as the suction on the rotating heads can be finicky.  Also some parts need a dab of epoxy under them to give them better mechanical adhesion to the PCB.  The epoxy needle failed often.

The main jobs were to keep the machines fed with part reels, to empty the receptacles that holds the plastic ribbon from the reels,  keep the carriages filled with PCBs, cleaning the solder masks periodically and repasting them, and finally visually inspect and then test each board.

Hey Steve! I have a suggestion for improving the fog box. Try to see if filling the box with it lying horizontally, such that the fill hole is on the side. The idea for this is due to top fill port in the upright position will force the fog to accumulate most of the density at the bottom section, and have less fog in the top of the box. You can see this when you open the door of the box the section nearest the table is nearly all white with fog, but the top is a mild haze. Of course the flow characteristics from the is the same with or without fog, but having a more even fog distribution could aid in the visualization of the flow in the case. To partially explain the AWS outage. What happened is that their East US data center went down. It went down because their internal services rely on their own product which was dynamo db. A large portion of their global services apparently then rely on the East US data center. So you had a cascading effect that a ton of AWS services were down regardless of your data center because their other service was down, and then on top of that, anything that was hosted in that data center also went down. 

So services failed because they had a single point of failure by relying only on AWS, and AWS was down because it had a single point of failure in a single data center, and the AWS data center was down because they had a single point of failure on one of their own services.

I ran a home lab (effectively) decades ago, now, and the benefits remain the same and pretty much what Wendell and Steve talked about.  The _negatives_, and they're real, are that you end up becoming a systems administrator.  Component failures, power outages, UPS backups, software upgrades (essential due to exploits), etc.  It's interesting stuff, teaches you a ton, and takes back control, but there IS a cost.  It's work, and it's why service companies exist. They can handle all of that at scale for cheap and that makes it appealing to use them - "It just works".  

This is not to say don't try a homelab, just be aware that there are "costs" associated with it, as well

This highlights a trend that I have seen over the last decade or more with new builds and the advice given to people who are just starting out, the lack of storage. We have normalized the idea that you only need a 1 or 2TB on your computer, you only need a single drive for the OS and all of your data, by only having one drive you save money to buy a more midrange GPU, etc...

We in the PC community need to start pushing the idea of having local storage in excess. For only $300 you can get 24TB of HDD storage so you can have your highspeed SSD for your OS and for your speed sensitive games and apps while being able to still have local bulk storage for everything else.

Fun fact: in professional visual effects and post-production, intermediate frame generation has been a thing for decades. It's mainly used to make super slow motion when the original footage couldn't be (or just wasn't) shot with a proper slow motion camera.

Despite not having to be rendered in real time (as in games), it also resulted in a bit of "shimmering" because the interpolated frames were never quite as sharp and detailed as the real ones.

So, how was this solved (in the visual effects industry)? Simple: by discarding all the real frames and replacing them with an interpolated frame based on the two adjacent interpolated frames. Yep. So, as soon as Nvidia adopts the same approach, we won't have to worry about _how many_ frames are fake, because the answer will be: *all of them.*

I've found that the results from Lossless Scaling depend a lot on the game. For instance, in Oblivion Remastered I found that the balance between smoothness, quality, and artifacts was best when using Lossless Scaling compared to FSR or MFG. In other games, FSR usually does the best job (I'm unable to use NVIDIA's latest MFG tech since I'm still using a 3090).

On my rig, I got the best results for 1440p ultrawide >120 fps (in most graphically intensive games) by changing the game's resolution to 2/3 of my monitor, windowed (so for my monitor: 2294 x 960), and then using auto in LS and the adaptive mode (meaning the LS scaling automatically at 3/2 or 150%) and the LS target framerate set to 120 in adaptive made, or higher when possible. This seemed to be the best balance of GPU performance between raw frames from the game render and upscaled + generated frames. Unfortunately, this means you have to manually adjust the game's config files, which can be hard to find and understand, and the files must be locked for the settings to be preserved (meaning you can't change them in-game afterward). If you're willing to go that deep, it might be worth it for a more optimized LS experience.

I feel like the video glossed over an important detail regarding LS's settings: the Capture API is important to keep in mind. LS has 2 options, DXGI and WGC. Usually both work just fine. But depending on the game, either can cause weird issues. In Hardspace: Shipbreaker, DXGI caused the game to run at a slower speed (inversly proportional to the FG multiplyer), switching to WGC fixed this. Other weird issues like the framerate metric showing weird results (240/240 when the game is clearly running < 60fps), so there's still a few bugs in LS to be aware of.

Overall it is really cool software that's fun to play around with and can give you a slightly better experience for some games, especially with relatively aged hardware (and at an insanely great price rn). Great overview and I look forward to seeing more!

I recently used Lossless Scaling in two games, Nier Automata and Clair Obscur, with *wildly* different results. I am using it on Linux via lsfg-vk, a community implementation for Linux, with 2x generation on both games.

Nier Automata (Steam) runs at a fixed 60 fps, with 30 fps prerendered cutscenes. In this game the results were very flakey, with a lot of environment textures artifacting extremely. My guess is that very low contrast due to fog effects is something LS's frame gen doesn't handle well. sometimes running through the desert looks a bit like a deep-fried meme. Overall I still vastly preferred it to straight 60 fps, especially since frame gen also works on the prerendered 30 fps cutscenes.

Clair Obscur can run with an unlimited framerate, but my PC can't get much higher than 60, and it also has 30 fps cutscenes. LS frame gen worked a lot better in this game, which I attribute to mostly higher contrast scenes. Even the 30 to 60 fps in cutscenes appears to work better, so overall image fidelity might influence results. (I'm still playing Clair Obscur btw, no spoilers please)

I feel like when you're getting into these use cases of cards designed as GPGPU from the ground up, we really need to stop calling them video cards or GPUs. In my project documentation, I generally just use the term "Math coprocessor" or GCPU (General Compute Processing Unit) since that's really what they're being used for in my use case. I guess "Math Coprocessor" or GCPU doesn't really roll off the tongue like "GPU" does (arguably better than GPGPU). Cards like this kind of remind of an evolution of the x87 FPU modules. They're not really alike in any way, but the idea of an expansion card purely for accelerated math processing via a more targeted architecture for parallelized loads isn't terribly far off a module with specific instructions/capabilities for expanding the machine's potential in calculation.

We had the problem seen at 30:45 while developing Horizon zero dawn. By running our physics engine at 60 Hz with a 59.95 Hz display, every so often the physics engine would be 'ahead' resulting in no updates for 2 consecutive frames. No lag spikes (less cpu work) but terrible animation error, really jarring. I worked on the animation tooling that all had to be updated to support different framerates to avoid the issue in cinematic playback as well, else it would drop a frame of data, but we never interpolated data, it was just baked out per-frame. I am glad we managed to fix it, though lag spikes still exist a big underlying issue was suddenly gone!

It might actually explain something I’ve noticed in CS2: some players say the game (especially AK spray) can feel more consistent when Reflex or Anti-Lag is turned off.

The idea is that these features try to keep the CPU and GPU perfectly in sync. But if there’s a short slowdown in the simulation — a few “slow” frames — Reflex/Anti-Lag may speed the game back up to stay in sync. That can cause sudden jumps in simulation speed, which might feel odd when aiming or spraying.

Without these features, the game just gets delayed slightly instead of trying to “catch up,” so you feel a bit more latency but fewer sudden shifts.

This “animation error” metric seems like it could make those effects visible.

Coming from the field of machine learning, this reminds of the challenges with model accuracy metrics, which are also a measure of error rates and magnitudes. When you need something between plotting all the data and distilling things to a single number (ala F-score), it's helpful to reach for plots which visualize distributions. For example, box and whisker plots. These show "at a glance" not only how bad errors gets, but how often. They may even work well with many on one chart.

Small addition on depth write information:

It is not (only) that a character behind an object is not being drawn (occluded). This is done by occlusion culling, and is done on the CPU or GPU before rendering.

Depth write (for depth testing) is used while rendering, and will discard pixels that would not be rendered because they're occluded.

It sounds similar, but where occlusion culling fully removes the object from the render pipeline, depth testing only removes the pixels that are not visible on screen, even if another part of that geometry is visible (partial occlusion)

Intel's GPUs have this behavior I have a love-hate relationship with. Their subgroup/wave/warp size is variable and has to be specified at pipeline compile time (unless you want to let the driver handle it, which is actually fine for most kinds of workloads that don't use subgroup ops). Most compute algorithms have settled on subgroups being 32-wide (thanks nvidia) because that lets you mask off all the threads using a single u32. Problem is, intel is the only IHV that also supports 16-wide subgroups, and they actually perform better than 32-wide due to register allocation/pressure reasons.

AMD used to do something similar prior to RDNA where their subgroups were 64-wide. Again, that's not a bad thing for most workloads, but it is when you're writing algorithms that depend on 32 invocations going simultaneously. The fix for that used to be to just mask off the top 32 of the subgroup, but that also means literally half the compute unit is doing nothing. Not good.

All this to say, intel focusing on 32-wide (SIMD32) performance is huge.

This event was super fun! Not everything in here is because of Windows 10 support ending; Kramden does this all the time, for any computer or reason. That's also why you see some Macs in here. Some more background if you're curious: Kramden gets a mix of e-waste and donated / retired machines from local individuals and from companies. Sometimes, these have perfectly good hardware, sometimes they have one or two broken things. They then work with volunteers (like in this episode) to reclaim anything valuable that could be used for education or cobbled-together into a new machine. A good example is the 12700K: This was in there because some company or person got rid of the computer, but obviously that's still a great part. The next step is to identify whatever was broken in the system, save the good parts, and repurpose them (or sell them to fund the classroom program). Anything unusable, such as just broken hardware or obsolete hardware, is broken down into recyclables and trash, sorted, and sent to the right groups to smelt down or dispose of. They are awesome.

For anyone curious about the "Super-Cores" thing, the channel Moore's Law is Dead leaked their existence and some architecture details a while back. They were under a project headed by Jim Keller called "Royal Core" which has since been killed/shelved. Over-simplification TL;DR: Under the hood, a modern CPU P-Core is not like one genius at one desk working one problem, it's like 10 people at one desk, each working tiny pieces of one problem. The idea was you could take these desks (cores) and dynamically allocate, split or combine their workers (execution ports).  For example: if each regular core has 10 workers, you could combine two of them into one high-performance core with double the workers and amazing single-thread performance, or split a core into two high-efficiency cores with half the workers each, and get amazing multi-thread performance.

intels idea has sooo many problems.
 1. a core cant execute ahead of a previous core if that core requires results from the calculations of the previous core. 
2. the overheads of working out what each core can do independently is going to be a nightmare. 
3. conditional branches will cause even more issues than on a traditional architecture. Either a core will execute code which is bypassed by a branch or a core or will have to wait until another core has worked out if the branch will be taken or not. 
4. obviously without locks on variables two cores will modify the same variable without knowing the other core has changed the value. 
5. traditional cores have pipe Ines so that they are decoding one instruction will running another while writing the results of another. This proposal either will have to have one pipeline for all the cores in a super core or make the pipelines much more complicated. 
6. this will probably need the compile to mark which sections can be executed in parallel independently. 
7. saving the processor state when there is a interrupt is going to be a nightmare.
8. deciding when to bound cores into a super core or split them is going to require look ahead, prediction and a scheduler. not to mention the overheads of adding and removing cores from a super core.
9. the operating systems cpu core scheduler already has a hard time with P cores and E cores on intel. Now its going to have to guess how many cores should be in a super core for how long. So the operating system scheduler is going to have even more issues.
10, cpu cache consistency is going to be a nightmare.

Intel already has 4 E cores sharing a single ring bus stop and L2. With Novalake this will expand to P cores with P cores being clustered into pairs.

In 3 or 4 generations, P cores will be gone and E cores will be scaled up in size to supplant P cores. This new unified core will be similar to how AMD does their standard and C cores: One core design that has a bigger higher clocking variant and the ability to make a smaller version with less clocks.

I presume Intel will still leverage their ring-bus and L2 sharing design with unified core. Super Cores are a great way to have a CPU alternate between a lot of weaker cores for embarrassingly parallel workloads, or to pair together and become ST monsters. It definitely has the possibility of being the most radical change to CPUs since the introduction of 3D stacked cache.

Hi Steve, some opinionated but maybe useful insight from someone who designed a bunch of zen 2 industrial motherboards.

I agree with the AMD engineer, PBO being the cause is completely bs. TDC and EDC aren’t there to protect the CPU, but to protect the motherboard, they’re there so that the CPU doesn’t try to suck in so much power that it pulls the voltage rails down.

My guess is that this is something you will only be able to confirm using a dummy load, which AMD is quite protective of, I couldn’t get one back in the day, but maybe you have more luck. 

I would bet a significant amount of money that the issue is that there’s either some fault in VRM routing or the component selection that is fine in nominal values, but fails when the tolerances stack up together. This could cause spikes during load transitions, which can easily kill the CPU. 

The problem with this is that not only you need a board that killed, you need all those parameters to “align” again, but most of those depend on temperature, some of them have hysteresis effects… in other words, a big fricking mess.

A couple of suggestions.
I feel the power supply used has to be included in the testing. Perhaps in some edge case, the power supply may send some spikes that the VRMS can't handle properly.
Another edge case, sometimes the ground prong in the power supply cable is cut off so it can fit older two prong sockets. This should be ruled out.

I have believed since the AM4 era that sudden CPU deaths are caused by undervoltage issues, although my view has often been dismissed. I recommend changing the **Power Supply Idle Control** option in the BIOS to **Typical Current Idle**.

With DDR5 adopting PMICs, the problem has become even worse. During the boot process, momentary undervoltage can cause boot failures (CPU and RAM error LEDs lighting up simultaneously) or unstable memory training that later results in stuttering.

If the CPU and RAM are exposed to such undervoltage spikes from the very beginning of the boot sequence, the system may still appear to boot normally, but it will continue to suffer from repeated voltage drops. Over time, this unstable condition stresses the VRM and the internal voltage regulation circuits (PMIC), leading to reduced stability margins. As a result, when attempting to deliver the same performance, current fluctuations (spikes) become more severe, and the accumulated stress eventually causes the CPU to fail.

Unstable booting may look fine to the user, but in reality, the VRM and PMIC are under heavy stress. I believe this repeated exposure to undervoltage is what damages the CPU.

It would be very useful if we could confirm that these momentary undervoltage events indeed cause cumulative damage to the CPU.

If you go a few decades back in time just about every computer case had integrated hardware to keep long card from flexing. It was a plastic stabilizer with a slot that was placed at the distance of a full length expansion card. Those would just slid into that slot as you put them in the machine. A full length expansion cards is about 340mm long and the last four or five millimeters are bare without any component so it can slide into the attachment. Cards like the the nVidia Quadro series was shorter, but came with a metal bracket that you screwed into the end of the graphic card and which fit into the slot in the stabilizer. 

This was standard was set with the IBM PC and were in all chassis for a long time. But lately it's only found in servers and workstations. Modern enthusiast machines totally lack support for this, and yet modern graphics card really need something like this to keep them from breaking the PCIe slot, themselves or both. And people cry over the lack of stabilization for the cards. Special stands are sold to prop them up and avoid the graphics card form bending by it's own weight, and some cases has suspension devices you screw into the case to hold the card in place. The simple solution would have been to reintroduce the standardized card retention that we used to have before they were discarded for cosmetic reasons. Sure they are not really all that good looking, but hey, they would make the computer a lot safer when you have to lug it around or if it's to be transported somewhere like being shipped to a customer. And it's not because of dimensions. Few graphics cards are longer than 340 mm, and if the retention had still been common then you can bet that the manufacturers would have ben able to make those cards fit the formfactor without really sacrificing anything but some plastic.

Great video, but here’s a few corrections/notes so newcomers don’t feel too intimidated:

1. For anyone waiting for SteamOS public release: Its components are available on every other distro, so you’re able to make your system very similar. Bazzite does this out of the box! Different names can be confusing, but really it’s the same technologies behind both.

3. Immutable doesn’t mean you can’t make changes to your system. You’re still free to change anything you want, they just make it harder to break and easier to recover if something breaks!

I switched to Linux a few years ago and will never switch back, but  the Linux community needs to understand that if they want Linux to grow in market share and influence they have to meet Windows/Mac users where they are to some extent. 

Distros like Bazzite currently achieve that fairly well. It's still Linux, but it's opinionated and has some important guard rails. A huge portion of people who are interested in switching to Linux don't care about or want full control over every little part of their system. They aren't enthusiasts, they aren't developers. They want to change the desktop wallpaper, adjust a few other fairly surface level options, and then just run the apps they want to run. The operating system should just get out of their way. If they have to think about it too much it's already a failure. 

If you think distros like Bazzite are violating some Linux philosophy or are a bad direction to go, that's okay. But you have to accept that from a desktop perspective Linux is never going to get beyond 5 or 6% market share without them.

1. DMCA Misrepresentation Claim (512(f))
The DMCA says if someone knowingly misrepresents that content is infringing, they’re liable for damages.
Case precedent: Lenz v. Universal (the “Dancing Baby” case). Court held copyright holders must consider fair use before issuing a takedown. If they don’t, that’s a misrepresentation.
For GN: Bloomberg would’ve had to intentionally ignore fair use (public speech + commentary). That’s a strong argument — it was a short excerpt of a public presidential speech, transformed in a documentary context.
Remedy: GN could sue for actual damages (lost revenue, costs) and possibly attorneys’ fees.

I've been through the process of learning in detail about YT's strike system several times at this point over more than 5 years by now and coincidentally Mr. French has been there each step of the way for me too, I see copyright on YT broadly the same as he does as a result. Having said that I want to point out that YT does not *fully* have free reign to just 'decide' how it's system works because there is a huge amount of grey area with how the DMCA and copyright law is specifically enforced and the companies *want* that grey area currently, to litigate it and establish a firm precident would potentially be disastrous and bring the fragile system down. As a result YT 'feels' a compulsion as a business to protect itself by erring on the side of claimants so that further action just never happens. So while yes, in principle they *could* come up with a more fair and just system they probably could not do so without either exposing themselves to more risk (even marginally so) *or* without spending more money on active moderation and policing, which would be the best outcome for probably everyone but that requires an effective monopoly to give up a fraction of their potential earnings so we know it's not likely to happen. 

What's that, you say? Generating positive creator sentiment by increasing confidence in the moderation system may, over the long run, result in increased profits due to that in turn increasing trust, content quality and then user sentiment/engagement and thus watch time? Don't be silly, we aren't allowed to be forward thinking when it comes to profit!

Re: writing thousands of USB keys simultaneously

several ways to do this:
1) find a USB replicator, no computer needed after the initial USB dongle is written. They exist, but they're hard to find and they're not necessarily affordable for small businesses
2) get a USB multiplexer that supports multiple output. Hard to find, but cheaper than a replicator and requires a computer to do the work
3) find a USB-C 3.1 Gen 2 hub with as many ports as you can afford that can actually do the full throughput speeds of the standard. You can get multiple hubs and put one on each USB controller on the mobo to get larger batches without losing speed. Setup a software RAID 1 in Linux for each batch of dongles.

I'm very happy with my Epoch case. I have a very specific case width constraint of <220 mm to fit in my older custom desk compartment. Back when my desk was made, that 220 mm width would easily fit a full tower. Modern cases have become fatter over the years thanks to the fascination with side panel windows and the need for more space behind the motherboard to hide cables. The Epoch is narrower than the competition and fits my space and my components perfectly. The Lian Li was also a consideration, but the Epoch can more easily fit a long 1600 watt power supply. The Epoch build quality is excellent. I went with basic black because RGB and side panel windows are a distraction.

Update: I built a pc for my son using the Corsair 4000D recently. In a head to head comparison, I still prefer the Epoch over the 4000D. The 4000D is more fiddly, routes all the front panel cables under the case in an ugly external bundle, and has external PCIe bracket thumbscrews with an awkward gap over the screws at the back of the case. The Epoch is simpler and cleaner.

Hi, long time subscriber here. I have a word about the compilation benchmark. Not sure you will read it, as I'm here when already over 500 comments are up, but at least I tried! ^^
I'm a software engineer, I've worked - among others - several years in the gamedev industry, where I have used daily a workstation with 12C/24T and later 16C/32T. 
To fully utilize the local machine during compilation of the Unreal Engine, we had to have 64GB of RAM - the build system was configured to spawn one job per thread, and each job required 1-1.5GB of memory. With 32 jobs x 1.5GB, opened IDE, browser, console management software and OS footprint, we were already at the edge of memory starving our compilation jobs.

With 64C/128T CPU I have a suspicion your 128GB RAM might be not really enough, especially given that we see relatively low uplift from 7960X (24C) to 7980X (64C), while the compilation of the large codebase is a task fairly parallelizable (at least before the consolidation phase time :). Of course there is a significant difference in the workload - different compiler, different build system, different codebase to be compiled, so we can't just apply constraints from Unreal Engine to the Chromium to conclude anything. But have you maybe tried to throw at it 256GB to see what would happen?

Hey Steve and Team,
the numbers from the convolution benchmark look reasonable. Applying convolutions boils down to applying a multiplications and addidtions to every pixel of an image. Processing them in batches with AVX512 speeds this process up. The new threadripper can use one AVX512 operation where the old one needed two 256-bit instrutions. We normally apply convolutions to images which fit into L3- maybe even L2-cache. So we won't get memory stalls which might hide these two 256-bit instructions. So fast data access and only one instructions leads to the 2x speedup.

But, I don't know if this applies to real world convolutions, because you normally would use a GPU for it. They are much faster and software is also highly optimized. Convolutions are common in Deep Learning tasks e.g. image classification. I don't know if editors like Photoshop use the GPU or CPU. Maybe they let you decide what you want to use.

There are many other real world task where we can use AVX512, e.g. file processing, databases, compression/decompression with certain algorithms, numerical computing. But i don't expect a speedup of 2x all the time. Often memory cannot keep up with the CPU so that the CPU must wait for the data. The convolution benchmark just hits a nice sweetspot, where we can see the AVX512 improvements and aren't hindered by the memory. I can go into greater detail, but this stuff gets very technical very fast, so i hope this was an good high level explanation. 

TLDR: The convolution numbers look good and are expected, but i would use a GPU in real world applications

Kind of the same story as the rest of Zen 5. Two-ahead branch prediction (which is wildly cutting-edge by the way), a fourth floating point pipe allowing for native AVX-512 support, another 2 Arithmetic Logic Units, and an expanded L1 data cache to support all that. These can be *extremely* beneficial upgrades for workloads that can make use of them, but a lot of real-world workloads are going to have bottlenecks elsewhere, so at the end of the day your mileage may vary. It's not like a die shrink generation where everyone gets a clock bump and a couple extra cores and the conclusion is easy to make. AVX-512 is pretty common at least in research software in my experience so the improvements there are likely a bit more relevant to the workstation crowd. There are relevant use-cases for AVX-512 in gaming so I'm somewhat curious if support will start to trickle down.

I’ve worked with metal my whole life, so I’ve seen firsthand how important it is to understand the right way to handle it. Because of that experience, I notice when there are constant misunderstandings or mistakes in how things are done. That’s why I’ve left these messages — to help highlight the issues and encourage better practices. I really hope they take this seriously and fix their methods for everyone’s benefit.

Just a heads-up to everyone working with liquid metal: even if it’s super pure, heating or agitating it can release fumes or microscopic particles that are seriously dangerous.

Some metals — like mercury, lead, zinc, cadmium, or even aluminum — can give off toxic gases or metallic particles when heated. These aren’t just mild irritants — we’re talking about vapors that can cause nerve damage, organ failure, or even death with enough exposure.

Even worse, if you breathe in metallic dust or fibers, those particles can lodge deep in your lungs and never leave. Over time, that can lead to chronic lung damage, metal fume fever, or long-term poisoning — often without obvious symptoms at first.

So if anyone’s mixing this stuff without a mask or ventilation, I’m not trying to call anyone out — but that’s genuinely unsafe. Doesn’t matter how pure the metal is — your lungs and body don’t filter out vaporized metal or microscopic fibers like that. Once absorbed, metals travel throughout the body and can accumulate in organs like the brain, liver, kidneys, and bones.
	•	This can lead to long-term damage, even if the exposure is small and repeated over time.
	•	The body can’t easily eliminate certain heavy metals, meaning they stay in your system and build up. This is a reason I would never work with chemicals directly, and even when I spray chemicals on my floor to wash them and I feel iffy about it because I have dogs with feet I basically switched to soap sprays now as they’ll absorb the chemicals into there paws 🐾 common sense

18:02 E-D-Schnellsieb isn’t a gas filter. It’s a nylon mesh strainer used to remove solid impurities from liquid metal, like oxides or slag. It doesn’t filter out any fumes or toxic gases at all.

If you’re working with molten metals, you still need proper ventilation and PPE to protect against metal vapor. That mesh won’t stop anything in the air from getting into your lungs.

It is vitally important that all those who signed the "Stop killing games" petitions do not regard the job as being done just because MPs/MEPs will be debating it.
This is just the start, and all those who want to see the purchases they made, or that others made, protected as their property, and the vendors held to account if they subsequently cripple something which has already been sold, must now contact their MP/MEP to give their views and demand that the same consumer protection enjoyed by the purchasers of other goods and services be extended to purchasers of software, including games.  If anything, there should be greater protection, as software cannot ever be said to be subject to "wear and tear" or other types of natural degradation.  The value of games individually doesn't matter - look at the size of the market overall to see the extent of the theft!  Just as if a criminal gang "only" demands £30 in protection money from a million users, it is a £30 million extortion, not a £30 one, and would be prosecuted as such.  Look up who your MP/MEPs is/are, and contact them at every stage in the process.  When it is formally accepted for debate, as soon as a date is set, immediately before the debate, and with reminders if any of these stages is more than a few weeks apart.  Make absolutely sure that they all know, and are not able to forget, that it is important to a large number of people, and that they will all be watching.

A couple of thoughts about this config. 

Buildzoid showed that tRAS doesn't really do anything on AM5 except make the system unstable when you set it too low, Performance is not affected having it higher. So generally you leave it high and then you play around with tRC to improve performance. 

It's also interesting to see that they played around with PBO (and although not featured in this video I'd like to see what they did with the curve optimizer) since it's been known to make CPUs appear stable but actually being unstable which can also affect the memory overclock. For an extra goldstar it would also be interesting to see if the tPHYRDL is matched between the DIMMs or not.

a few constructive comments and feedback about LM studio testing,
1) generally when nvidia cards start giving 5-6 tokens per second it means you are partially offloading some of the work from vram to normal ram and involve the cpu, in those cases you want to include some partial offloading label since you are not longer just testing the gpu

2) in related to that comment, the context length you set drink up a lot of the vram , so a 30gb model with 500 context length will take 31gb vram and manage to stay on the 5090, but a 30gb model with 4000 context length will leak out of the 32gb and will partially offload to normal ram making tokens per second much slower, 

3) add a label much like you do with what setting you use in video game on what setting you used for the LM studio model so we can follow along and verify results if needed or have a way to test ourself

for future benchmarking with LLMs, I would recommend comparing tokens/sec of the card being tested to a multi-card system. For example, using Ollama, it's pretty easy to build a 2, 3 or 4 GPU machine and Ollama splits the model across the cards auto-magically. For example, I sourced four 3090s from ebay and built a rig that has the four 3090s (24 x 4 = 96 GB VRAM) and can easily run the llama 70B model in-memory.

For example on my 4x3090 rig (which isn't highly optimized) I get 16.75 tokens/second from the llama 70B model vs what appears to be ~29 tokens/second for the RTX Pro 6000.

I'll leave it up to others to decide if the RTX Pro 6000 at ~29 toks/sec is better than ~16 toks/sec on my ~$4K rig (all in cost, cpu motherboard, GPUs, ram, PSU). For me personally, once a model runs above 10 tok/sec, it's generating text faster than I can read it. For non-direct reading use cases, higher toks/sec would definitely be more important (API, Agentic work flows, etc)

I remember as a recently graduated EE in the mid 90's that all the computer companies were desperate to attract RF engineers. The reason being as clock speeds increased suddenly a lot of the rules started changing because at a higher frequency minute capacitances and inductance really starts to matter.  For instance if you have 32 lines to memory they all have to be electrically the exact same length and the same impedance and the higher the frequency the more it matters. The guys that had that knowledge at that time were all RF engineers that worked with microwave (1 GHz and above) frequencies. Now the structures are so small that you are getting into the realm of having to have knowledge of particle physics.
I can't comprehend this tech, just like I can't understand how the universe is infinite. This is pretty much magic. People taught rocks to think.

Im an EE and I regularly do PCB designing work... Actually making the substrate is easy. Its just a PCB design the scammers could get them made with anyone and even populate the capacitors for them...  There really isnt anything to it there other than looking at a "real" chip and trying to copy its layout.
One reason the substrate colour looks different is not only a slightly different blue dye, but also that theres a ground layer on that pcb. The copper makes it darker... 
The little lighter dots you saw are vias in the substrate. stitching that ground layer across the other ground layers the board has. 
Everything else you spoke of are just manufacturing tolerances of the PCB fab the counterfeits were made at.

The real data matrix is 20x20 (so the data part is 18 x 18). The fake one is smaller: 18 x 18 (data part is 16 x 16). This has 18 data bits and 14 ECC bits. I decoded the first 18 chunks as "56KR1382Q30654c260m003200514" Plugging this into a code generator online has completely different error checking bits. This is why it fails to scan (although my phone recomputes the data matrix differently so maybe I don't know here). Whatever the case, I did confirm that I got the first 18 chunks (all the data) correct.

Interestingly enough, the AMD one has only 17 chunks, so they could have fit it in a smaller data matrix than the one they used. Instead they have 17 chunks and 5 chunks of padding. Doing the math out, if the entire serial number were alternating numbers and letters, that's the exact length that will fit. (the data matrix saves a chunk for each pair of numbers, so 411260 takes up three chunks 41, 12, 60)

I'm honestly not sure where they got this Data Matrix, it would have been a lot easier to just copy the AMD one 1:1 or use the serial number on the chip itself.
Is there another AMD CPU out there with serial number 56KR1382Q30654?
Maybe they did the data matrix for the above serial number (the first one they faked) didn't notice that it was padded and then lasered in that to all the chips with a different made-up serial number on the rest?

Just built in this case and it was a breeze. Some things to be mindful of for potential buyers:

1) The spec sheet says it supports a sideways-mounted PSU of up to 180mm long, but the 175mm one I bought would have made for some uncomfortable cable bends so I wound up mounting it the regular way. If you're dead set on using this feature, either because you think its cool or because you want to use all the ungodly number of drive mounts the case supports, I would follow Steve's advice and get a 150mm standard-length PSU. 

2) The GPU anti-sag bracket attaches to a metal strip that bends into the case and I had to loop the USB cable for the front panel through it in order to connect it to the MB's side-facing connector. It still worked for me but the cable placement could interfere with properly positioning the bracket depending on where your board's connectors are. If that spot on the MB is loaded with connectors you plan on using you may be better off getting a third party bracket/supporter. 

3) The length of the anti-sag bracket also had it colliding with a GPU fan (there are two slots where you can mount it and it hit in both positions), so I wedged one of the extra rubber fan grommets that came with the case between the bracket and the GPU to give it the needed clearance.

The thing I hate most about this "8GB is enough for 1080p" is that it's a bunk argument to begin with. It assumes that resolution is the end all be all of keeping within a VRAM buffer. 1080p in 2025 is not the same as 1080p in 2016 when the 1060 came out. Many many options are just as or more demanding on VRAM in modern games as resolution. If a game is running at the same settings and you only change the resolution to 1440p or 4k the difference isn't going to be 8gb, it's going to be 2-4gb. Which is why 12gb runs 1080p games flawlessly regardless of settings while 8gb requires multiple compromises. 

This is also going to get worse because, as we've seen in the last 8 months or so, more and more games are coming out without the option to fully disable RT effects. RT gobbles up VRAM far worse than resolution does. This is only going to get more and more common with each release as devs streamline their workload to stop supplying two bespoke lighting solutions for every title. I mean RT's been around for 6 years, the transition has to happen at some point. Whether hardware is ready or not doesn't mean squat to publishers because they really don't care if a game runs well or not. Turn on DLSS or FSR if you want 30 fps is all they'll say.  

Also, the focus on "esports titles" is also BS. A toaster can run those in excess of 100 FPS at 1080p. You don't need a new card for that. Literally any video card made since 2019 can blast through Esports games. It's a nonsense talking point. Hell, if you buy a now nearly 10 year old 1080ti you'd tear through every single esports title and you'd get 11gb of ram to boot. The Esports gamer doesn't need to upgrade unless they are running something incredibly low end. What would these 8gb cards even be an upgrade from? They run about just as well as 3060ti from 4 years ago and that had a 12gb model. They'd be better off buying one of those used. Or you know, consoles and phones also have most esports titles and run them just fine because, again, a toaster can run them.

So, this entire conversation comes immediately from a place of dishonesty and hyper focuses on something that's not as relevant as they'd like you to think (resolution) or are already completely irrelevant (esports discussion) and will become more and more irrelevant going forward. I hate all of it, the whole conversation is crap and everyone just goes along with the faulty framing AMD/Nvidia is pushing for justifying 8gb in 2025.

I own a motherboard from Asrock, specifically the b650 livemixer. Fortunately, I've been using my 9600X for almost 6 months without problems. But after watching this video, I realized that Asrock's Vice President doesn't know the cause of the failures, since PBO was disabled for many who encountered processor burnout. Before this, I had a sad experience with a motherboard from Maxsun - it burned my 7500F processor after enabling the Expo profile at 6800 MHz (there's a video on my channel). Now I see that history is repeating, but with Asrock. Considering the fact that most burned processors were either in idle state or sleep mode.

I think there's a problem with power saving modes and their impact on vSOC. I would like to recommend not using the Expo profile, but setting all values manually. Don't exceed 1.25 volts on vSOC. And preferably use fixed voltage and frequency, if cooling and the chip itself allow it - in my case, I fixed the frequency at 5.5 GHz with 1.265 Volts, reducing the maximum voltage by 100 mV, and lowering temperatures from 77 to 67-70.

I have an Asrock board and had a defective 9800x3D. System initially worked fine on the BIOS the board came with (EXPO on, rest stock), then froze 2 days in. Red CPU error LED was lit, couldn't get it to boot, only managed to after many flashback attempts. It ran for 5 hours, then froze again. Eventually, it seemed as if it would start if the PC was off for a while before freezing again after 10 minutes at the latest. Perhaps residual current from an overcurrent that needed to dissipate? EXPO made no difference. I had two bluescreens that pointed to memory controller issues, so I RMAed the CPU and, with the new CPU, it now runs fine. Of course, I cannot tell if that is due to being on the current BIOS since the new CPU never ran on the old one, or if the original BIOS degraded the old CPU, but this is just an anecdote I wanted to add to this whole discussion. A data center I was working for around 20 years ago experimented with immersion cooling one year. We used a discarded retail reach-in freezer body for the chamber but had better luck with fluid-optimized heat exchanger cores and flowed the cooling fluid through the cores for radiative cooling, then fed the discharge into a large commercial chiller unit to recirc. The hoses are fairly standard industrial-sized reefer hoses with what look like quick disconnect fittings. 
To retrofit 200-odd server racks was deemed more costly than using the existing 10C ambient air room cooling 24/7/365 strategy and trying to leverage into on-site produced 'renewable' energy. (They were still pulling several MW/month and I'm sure the wind turbine was there for tax credits).

Immersion cooling was talked about and shown pretty much a decade or two back. I remember that one problem was that they had to make sure the hard drive wouldn't leak so the ventilation holes were sealed. The liquid used was most often food grade oil, I think it was mineral oil, and they usually worked well for a while. The computer would mostly work until they needed to swap some component like a graphics card. But draining, refilling and handling the components drenched in mineral oil usually meant the users did away with immersion cooling after a while. It was fun while it lasted but it also made water cooling look ridiculously simple and effortless. And then there were the unfortunate that had components degrade as they reacted with the oil or the entire fish tank would start leaking as the oil reacted with the glue keeping the tank together.

I almost think crossflow fans would make sense to put horizontally into the PSU shroud because they can pull a lot of air into a much more comparatively thinner footprint in that application compared to an axial fan. This would mean providing direct airflow for the GPU while taking up (comparatively) minimal additional space inside the case, and with fewer compromises to functionality of the rest of the case. The only downside to that would be needing to put vents on the side of the case that is typically where you have a transparent material like tempered glass, but plenty of cases already have ventilation on the side PSU shroud anyway so I see this as an easy thing to adapt.

This configuration is interesting, but I feel it makes too many compromises for what it achieves. It doesn't seem to leverage the advantages of the crossflow fan, but rather seeks to replace axial fans in some capacity, which to me doesn't make sense. A horizontally-mounted GPU intake fan that pulls air from a ventilated PSU shroud to me makes far more practical sense.

Don't know if TRYx is going to bother reading any of these comments, but we have been using laminar flow fans in reef tanks (saltwater fish tanks) for years.  If they want to apply that same concept in CPU cases moving air instead of saltwater they really need to think harder about the flow path throughout the case.  Spend the extra $ it will cost them per case and add 1 top exhaust fans, 1 rear exhaust fans and 1 bottom intake.  Not only will it test better in the GN testing, but it will cool better across the board and if people end up using an AIO in the top (side intake will likely test better in this case layout), they can always move the second fan somewhere like the bottom below the graphics card where it would benefit from being regardless.

Truthfully, my first setup I would try if air cooling would be no front intakes, 3 side intakes, 2 top exhaust 2 bottom intakes 1 rear exhaust + the laminar flow front intake.  If AIO, AIO side intake, and add a 3rd top exhaust.

If they need the additional front fans to lower temps then the implementation of the laminar flow design is just gimmicky and unnecessary.  Best performance is probably 1 laminar flow intake on each side of the front but not only does that skyrocket the cost it also removes side intake/rad support.

Laminar flow is great, but you have to really consider how you plan to make those directional changes when using it, hence most laminar flow fish tanks still have to have small traditional fans for "dead spots".  If you're going to apply it in a PC case, where do you want to force the laminar flow to turn when it needs to SHOULD be the design goal.

For anyone who is worried and has a motherboard that can do this, I do this.

1. I have a temp sensor cable from my motherboard to the 12VHPWR connector. (I have Aida64 running)
2. I played the most demanding games I have, with the highest power draw (Cyberpunk maxed out) and took note of the temperature on the sensor, even though some of that will be the case temperature warming up, not just the connector. This is so I have a worst-case high temp.
3. Next, I set Aida64 to warn me once the temperature sensor hits that temperature. I also have one set 10c even higher that shuts off my PC should it hit that temperature.

Because of this, I will either get the warning and check, or if I am away from the PC and the second temp is reached, it will turn my PC off.
Due to the room temperature, the only thing I have to do is have one base temperature for the summer and one for the winter.

Dynamic balancing. As opposed to static, stationary, where you add or remove mass from an object suspended in a bearing system, until no one side is heavier(it would otherwise slowly rotate until heavier side is down). While dynamic accounts for the location of the mass in the 3rd axis, along the axle, where it might cause axle wobble. In order to measure this, it must be spinning. Cool.

The balancing is similar to how they would balance your wheels after a tire change/replacement.

You're looking for uneven rotating inertia, due to uneven mass distribution as a result of production (for all of the reasons that Tenzin mention (and there are a whole bunch more that he didn't explicitly mention as well), and you do that in a dynamic environment.

From the engineering side of things, you actually run statistical models to throw/introduce randomness into your perfect CAD design, and then you evaluate/run the statistical analysis to look for compatibility/interference/clash issues as well as durability issues

The statistical process controls for injection moulded parts is unlike any other, because there are just more variables that you have to consider with the entire injection moulding process in and of itself. Plastics process engineers have their work cut out for them, and trying to do the plastics process engineering reliably and in a predictable fashion so that you can deploy countermeasures for any potential manufacturing issues is half-art-half-science.

The CPU and motherboard components would not be heated by the GPU which, in theory at least, would result in the best overall cooling possible even if an air cooling solution was used instead of liquid cooling. A separate chamber for the GPU or GPUs and associated cooling solutions(s) would be an ideal solution.

Triple Chamber design is a great concept. I like the idea of moving the side panel mount to the front, then forcing the air to the side as an exhaust. But ducts are hard to work with for the average consumer. The back 120mm fan requiring a bracket that has it sitting slightly on the glass side panel is a bit annoying too. If they offered a mesh side panel that had mounting holes, would be nice. The back panel on the standard "Dual Chamber" portion could use some extra mesh as well, the square mesh isn't doing it enough justice I think.

Phase change (boiling) engineering actually gets SUPER complicated because you have "micro" pockets of phase change happening, which causes all KINDS of problems.

(In boat propellers, localised boiling due to rapid changes of motion of the propeller itself, causes caviation (drop in pressure), which is enough to PHYSICALLY damage said propeller blades.)

You don't cover that in neither your 4th grade science classes nor even in your 3rd year thermo/fluid dynamics classes.

It is crazy/ridiculous how complicated the entire act of "boiling" can be.

(And then to model it accurately, people have literally gotten Ph.D.s just to study this thing called "boiling". You' never look at boiling potatoes nor making hard boiled eggs nor making ramen (in a pot), the same.)

that small wire connecting pins on top of the PCB is called enamelled copper. Basically, it's copper inside, but it has an electrical insulator outside. These types of wires are used for "reworks": a common procedure during development and/or pre-production, when a PCB is made in small quantities for validation and, before a new version is printed, maybe an older version can just be slightly reworked instead of asking a PCB maker to print it out again. Saves a lot of time as long as those reworking the PCB know what they are doing.

The shroud results actually make perfect sense. The narrow, but aerodynamic shroud pushes air into a specific area, where it cannot be properly utilized to move air around the entire GPU - you need to be able to force air exiting GPU cooling to move away from it. The difference is marginal, because standard flat shrouds have holes, which allow the air from under the shroud to be pushed up.

One rather pedantic comment: Coherency in CXL allows multiple hosts to access (and cache) the same CXL memory without introducing errors, such as some host reading stale data from the shared CXL memory pool because the latest version of that data is in another host's cache. In this way memory coherence ensures that all hosts sharing memory from a pool see consistent data, which is hard, again, because hosts can modify data in local caches without writing it back to memory.
