The example coolers they gave you to compare with is 4 standard heatpipes vs 2 3dhp but i feel like it makes more sense for larger coolers, like the Noctua example, that has 6 or more heatpipes. 

Once you start getting more heatpipes in one cooler it gets harder to fit them on top of the heat source, the die, and the outer heatpipes won't have as great of contact. A cooler with 6 3dhps has 18 "risers" up into the fin stack while a cooler with 8 standard heatpipes has 16 "risers" into the fin stack. So even if you can bend the standard heatpipes to evenly distribute the heat into the fin stack, the 3dhps allow for more risers while having the base of the heatpipes more centrally located on the heat source.

I'm not a heatsink engineer but it seems like these 3dhps will be most useful in larger heatsinks because of what I described, though larger heatsinks requires more heatpipes which of course exacerbates the described yield issues.

in this experiment, i think the most likely explanation for why the new "3DHP" shed heat faster is because of it's greater surface area. the experiment compared 1 standard heat pipe (with 2 risers) against the 3DHP which has a similar surface area to 1.5 standard heat pipes (3 risers). for a heat exchanger, Q = U * A * ΔT. in this experiment that removed the fins to isolate the heat pipes, the surface area of the heat pipes is what transferred heat from the condensing fluid to the surrounding air. A of the standard heat pipe was about 2/3 of the A for the 3DHP. i expect future testing of similarly sized air coolers with the same number of heat pipe risers (like the example in the video showing noctua's heat pipes distributed throughout the fin stack) will demonstrate that this new design will not result in better performance for an air cooler. i think GN's testing of other factors show that they matter more for competitive advantages, such as flatness of the contact area, surface area of the fins, etc. heat pipes are cool! fun content!

She picked it because she liked the aesthetic and the look of the optional front panels that Corsair said they'd sell (they're still not available). I ended copying her and getting the black version of the case for my own build because I was so impressed with it while building hers. It was super easy and fun to build in and just barely fits my liquid freezer III. Love the GPU fans on the PSU shroud. So excited to see you guys do a review! Aesthetic tip, on my girlfriend's build we managed to install both the side intake fan brackets with two fans AND the cable cover bracket, I don't believe Corsair intended this to be an option but it's quite easy to do. She didn't like the look of the two extra black fans that we had so putting the cable over in front of them blocked them from view outside of the case and directed their air flow directly at the motherboard and ram at the cost of reducing their efficiency. There's about an 1.5"-2" between the back of the fan and the cable cover on a standard 120mm fan, not optimal but it's still allows for air flow. Not for everyone, on my build I personally have all 3 slots filled without the cover as intended by Corsair. I just figured it could be useful information for someone who really didn't want to see side intake fans but wanted the additional air flow for positive pressure or whatever.

The main issue with ARM is the lack of a straightforward ISA.  In x86 land I can take a system disk out of one x86 box with an i7 and plug it into a Ryzen CPU machine with completely different underlying hardware and everything baked into that OS and the software on top just works once the kernel loads the correct drivers.  ARM is a forced march of obsolescence due to ISA inconsistency where there are portability problems within the same generation of hardware with the same SoC. Last week I was speaking with a hardware vendor in the 3D printing space that their specialty display part (mSLA) will work with a RPi CM4, but not other Pi4 psuedo-clone hardware and isn't even forwards compatible "today" with RPi CM5. This btw, is why you see CM4s priced close to CM5 hardware -- the CM4 took off well enough and is used enough places where a CM5 will not simply drop in as an upgrade. The development cycle starts very nearly from scratch. 

The embedded systems are awful for long term support if you want a product to develop and evolve. While this doesn't matter for an HVAC system, if say we're talking about automative with driver assistance features, this means issues with base OS updating -- Linux, QNX, and whatnot -- validation among board revisions, much less generation to generation compute platforms is a complete mess. 

I won't even get into my day job, but suffice it to say, I deal with specialized hardware currently moving TO x86 to get away from generation-to-generation incompatibility and feature change in other CPU architectures. 

Most of the excitement I have seen in the software development community is about making software development work more ephemeral. They can label it as avoiding x86 "legacy" and "cruft", but it feels very "new shiny" and the real appeal of ARM platforms is **zero commitment.** A year later, they wave their hands and say, "obsolete" and walk away from a platform. We see this across a wide variety of consumer products well outside of the easy target in modern phones with limited support lifecycles. 

Every piece of TV, AV, IoT running ARM similarly is incredibly short-lived, and unlike x86, can't be opened up and extended or repurposed. In the embedded space with ARM + Linux, we see devices with let's say USB camera "capability", but inconsistent *compatibility* where it has a stricter approved hardware list than the NT 4 HCL.

RISC-V is taking the same path ARM has (embedded controllers first to build tooling and a history of reliability) and is both free to license and allows for much more customized implementations, leading to a huge amount of innovation. Nvidia alone has already shipped over 1 billion RISC-V cores.

When will ARM reach the point where you can just download a Linux distro and boot from a flash drive?

Currently x86 is just plug in a drive and it works because of ACPI. Consumer ARM currently requires a device tree to first be made to discover the hardware on that specific motherboard before you can run it. Plus some manufacturers such as Qualcomm on their mobile chips limit up to what Linux kernel you can run.

ARM is awesome, but we need to reach a point where you can buy a 10 year old secondhand device and still run a recent operating system on it.

Will ARM ever reach a point where you can just boot an operating system you've just downloaded without it using an image specifically tailored for your device?

x86 is alive and well by mistake. Intel is probably fuming on the engineering team for creating the boot system that even UEFI could not fix - it gives you freedom to install any OS you want without a risk of bricking your PC.
ARM is the primary hardware for Anrdoid. Android is an OS designed to work on every hardware (including x86), on any screen (touch or not), with any input. Android should have been the ARM OS everyone would use in 2020s and the future, yet, it is a toy OS for toy devices (I mean phones). And it is like that for one reason only - (corporate) "security", or "don't use your device the way manufacturer did not intent to".
The problem for ARM desktop can go either way. They can go to the opensource way preventing a CPU locking of OS, or they can go the Android way and be "secure". If the former happens, the only difference between x86 and ARM would be, it would provide freedom to users by design, not by mistake. But if it goes to the path of "security", Intel is not screwed and x86 won't die for now.

I used to work at a bicycle frame building company and there was usually 2 or 4 TIG welding stations in operation throughout the day and we had this massive, droning box hanging from the ceiling that used electrostatic, electromagnetic filter mediums in addition to particulate centrifugal and paper filter media to clean the air. TIG welding releases a lot of toxic Iron, Chromium and Molybdenum microdust and smoke.

  In this environment a clean air space means the welds are less contaminated, stronger and you use a little less shielding gas.

 And as a side benefit, you as an employee are breathing air that's much cleaner than even the outside air.   This was in an area locally known for it's Spring and Summer pollen, and Fall/Winter soot and mold spore counts.  It was awesome to work at.   I was also a lot younger and rode my bicycle to work frequently, had less allergy days and was generally healthier.

I really don't want to look into the case all the time and hate the idea of having entire side panels made of glass that can break if there's some simple accident. A friend has one computer with a broken glass side panel, but luckily he hadn't pulled the plastic protection film so that held it together. Now he has reinforced the plastic on the outside by putting tape over the inside so the panel is sandwiched between the  plastic protection film and the tape. Since Steve seemed interested in vacuum pumps, the reason you need a second stage for high vacuum (so low pressure) is all based on mean-free path.  That just means on average how far a particle goes before colliding with something.  At low vacuum you can just use a pretty standard pump because air is a fluid and we call it a roughing pump.  At some point though you start having to treat the remaining air as individual particles and so diffusion instead of fluid mechanics dominate and that requires a completely different pump structure.  Plus even your basic vacuum lubricants will start to evaporate at some low vapor pressure and that limits how high of vacuum you can go while also potentially contaminating your sample.

A turbo pump is literally just multiple layers of fan blades spinning typically around 40k-50k RPM so that any particle a blade hits will get deflected downwards and away from the vacuum chamber.  Multiple stages of those blades just helps to create an overall useful pressure differential across the entire pump and prevent molecules from escaping back into the chamber.  There are other types like a diffusion pump that shoots oil vapor out and downward to do the same thing or a cryopump that relies on trapping some gasses by condensing them onto a surface chilled typically by helium so you can get very cold.  A lot of times you can even combine these such as having a nice cold surface cooled by liquid nitrogen that acts as a cryotrap by reducing the kinetic energy of molecules so they hang out down near a diffusion pump for longer and are more likely get to get pushed out.

In any case though a high vacuum pump doesn't work under low vacuums and more importantly can only handle a relatively slight pressure differential across the pump.  So behind that high vacuum pump you'll have a backing pump that can push those molecules out into atmosphere.  Usually that is just your same roughing pump and you just use a valve so the roughing pump stops getting exposed to the chamber pressure but instead to the back end of the high vacuum pump.

Why all this is necessary is for electron microscopes goes right back to mean-free path but this time for electrons.  You need sufficiently high vacuum so the electrons hit your sample instead of air molecules, and the same for electrons emitted from the sample to get to the detector.

In Britain, we had our own attempt at tariffs. In the 70s, the bulk of our cars were, frankly, absolute shite. This was mostly in the West Midlands and generally known as British Leyland. The Japanese made drastically better cars, for less money, the Germans made better, and higher end, cars for the same money and the British arm of Ford (still American, but quite different to US Ford at the time) were also much better. Instead of British Leyland not being shit and making better cars (it didn't help that everyone was going on strike at the time), the government decided that the best thing to do would be to step in and tariff all foreign car manufacturers. The end result? British Leyland deservedly went bust and, fifty years later, we *still* pay 2-3 times as much for the same vehicles as any other country, because the tariff prices just became the standard price here.

Long term tariffs do not work, and we have many examples of this. When used within reason, subsidies are a much better option for a number of reasons, though they're not a perfect solution either, especially in the eyes of full on free marketeers.

funny thing, when wendel mentioned that he would like mainboards to have hardware switch or jumper for flashing bios, i assume he was reminiscing things from the past, because "write enable" bios jumper was a thing in old days. first bioses were sitting in roms, later in eproms (which your would need first clear with uv light, then flash with programmer), somewhat later, they switched to EEPROM, you would boot from floppy disk and flash bios, but to be able to do that, you need to flip dip switch, or move jumper on board, to be able to write. later they replaced hardware switch (i think i've seend that first on pentium boards), with setting inside bios itself. and what we have now (or rather for at least 15 or more years) are bioses you can flash by utility that you can run from windows, with 0 protection. of course we also have dualbios system (where you flash one bios slot, and other remains the old one, so system will boot to older one in case of fatal failure), also "bios flash" buttons on mainboards, but all those things are unprotected. on server boards you usually need to login into IPMI or equivalent to be able to flash bios, but on consumer boards. heck hp is known to deliver faulty bios trough windows update, that bricked people notebooks. so i get the sentiment to have physical barier for bios flash.

Given the potential for damage if given absolute freedom like there is now, it probably makes sense to have one layer that allows simple overrides that the system can, itself, override in the event of overheating or overstress or something. Small nit: only rings 0 and 3 are in actual use on at least Intel x86 (and 64). Other CPU architectures also have rings (especially IBM s390x), but their layout and limitations wildly differ. On Intel, other rings were proposed, IIRC up to 7, but they were largely ignored, and industry actually went the other way around, with informal "negative" rings (which are mostly reserved for virtualization stuff and AMD PSP/Intel ME microcode having much more access to underlying hardware and abstracting stuff for ring 0).

Not sure if anyone from the video will see this, but there is a way to pause updates indefinitely if you want. Windows will suspend updates if a third-party patch tool requests to manage updates. There is a free tool called Action1 you can sign up for. If you put its agent on the system and do updates through Action1 a single time, you can ask it to deactivate Windows Update and it will do so as it takes over patch management. Even if you never update with Action1 again, that should keep Windows from updating and not needing constant deferrals. However, you can also use it to do granular patch approvals as well, which allows you specific control over what gets installed. Free for up to a number of endpoints much larger than you guys would need and their agent is extremely light weight. Hope this helps.

With the newest Hotfix driver 576.66 driver you can experience a permanent no signal bug, mainly on 30XX cards. 

If you install and after the necessary restart you will most likely experience one random signal loss, even in idle before it's fully booted!
In 9/10 cases the signal loss is permanent, no matter how many times you hard reset, replug it, use a different monitor, whatever it stays. 
I've tested it with 10 various PCs with slightly similar hardware (all Intel 13k CPUs, all 30xx) and had on 9/10 PCs this issue. 
The only two ways to get the signal back is to use the iGPU or by unplugging your GPU(s) from power and your Mainboard, boot the PC, do a hard shut down, put them in again, boot up and connect the monitor.

However, if you are using the 1. option but still have a monitor connected to the GPU and/or the GPU still powered up and connected to the mainboard the random signal loss can still happen, same with the 2nd option.

It very rarely happens if you are in the bios.

Electrical Engineering PhD student here: one thought about that ASUS connector. I would be very curious how they are reliably transferring 600W through that connector. The main issue is that the “fingers” of the PCI-E connector are just the copper of the pcb left exposed then gold plated to ensure good electrical connectivity. Typically the copper of the PCB is not very thick and thus for things like power rails we might leave the solder mask off so that when the board goes through the soldering machine, it builds up solder on the exposed traces so that there is essentially a wire on top of the board for higher current carrying capability. However, with that connector, that would not be an option as it is physically constrained… They could of course make the outer copper layers for the whole PCB much thicker, but that would be prohibitively expensive I would think. Also to my knowledge you can’t make just one section of the board have thicker copper. So maybe they are using a small daughter board that utilizes thicker copper? Obviously they could make the traces wider to be able to carry more current but the width I was seeing didn’t seem anywhere near wide enough for 50 amps.

I’m just waiting for the day when we swap to 48V instead of 12V for the main supply voltages in computers so that we don’t have to deal with these absurd currents 😂 (600W/12V = 50A vs 600W/48V= 12.5A)

Got a few things to clarify here. Neither the laptop, nor the cooler is made by XMG. It's made by an OEM called Tongfang and many companies (XMG, Eluktronics, PCSpecialist, Medion, Tuxedo, etc...) sell it under their name. The laptop is configurable to order when bought with various gpus and for easier manufacturing the motherboard was made modular last year (this liquid cooled series is running since 2021)
The cooler itself is in its 3rd generation (or 4th rev), and pretty underwhelming to see they started to use the magnetic connection for the unit. I've got a 2023 model, and in that, the cooler end is properly secured with a screw-on seal, the laptop side is magnetic which interestingly although bad but still works better than this one in the video(the only issue it has is that the tube can pull it down, but only if the laptop it's on a vesa stand like I have, on a table it's not a problem). 
Also it doesnt do wonders, but really helps with having sustained performance without the laptop sounding like a hair dryer, more so given that the new generations has way quieter pump and fan than mine has. Also these cooling units are interchangeable between generations, and they connect to the laptop via bluetooth
Also interesting to see that under 2 years they blocked off a lot more openings on the bottom of the unit, the 2023 one had less cool design went on the bottom plate but looks to have way better throughput(and honestly made me nervous that it sucks a lot of dust in)

The separate MB and GPU board probably allow them more flexibility during manufacturing.

They can make one MB solution, and pair it with different GPUs easily. A good way to hedge against inconsistent supply of any specific GPU.

Probably helps with manufacturing defect repairs on the production line. You are not risking both the CPU and GPU at the same time when sending a faulty board to the repair line.

The reason laptops have low porosity on the bottom is for fan protection. Being a laptop, it is meant to be used in all kinds of environments with uneven ground and uneven pressure applied. Dude with a Steamworks account here. The way uploading builds works is that once you're past the initial build review, you're free to upload builds without any further checks by Valve, which will be instantly available to all users. You're not even forced to use the reviewed build as the one you launch with.

I would like to assume that Valve has some automatic scanning on their servers, though heuristics and detected generic variants such as in this case might be not considered precise enough to automatically raise alarms. I have pushed a build before that had a false positive in Windows Defender of all things. However from the detected name, it seemed like it was a machine learned heuristics detection. Thankfully this was cleared up fairly quickly on Microsoft's end, but on Valve's side nothing happened.

As for this "game"'s case, while it's not a real security barrier, I feel like as a defense in depth it might be a decent idea to set your firewall to default deny for outgoing connections. It doesn't seem like any privileges were escalated and only user accessible access tokens were stolen? In that case the malware would've had trouble to whitelist itself to call home at least. As long as there wasn't more to it, I suppose. And since that configuration is rare, maybe it wouldn't be smart enough to handle it either.
Of course having it on default deny comes with a few annoyances, but it's doable after jumping over the initial hurdles.

At the end of 2023, I decide to spend time looking at reviews and start getting reacquainted with PC components. My last gaming rig was built in 2002 and I had not been able to find a sweet spot to get back into PC gaming with all the many issues over the last few years. Since then, I’ve watched every CPU and GPU review from GN.

My biggest complaint with GN reviews over the last year and a half or so, is that telling me to just “not buy” a particular GPU or CPU is not helpful. I don’t have current hardware to replace so telling me to just stay put on my current rig is not encouraging.

Obviously NVIDIA has had other issues other than just not being worth it for the price, but when the previous Gens can’t be bought at a price point that makes them worth it, someone like me is expecting to be informed of what options are available.

All this to say, maybe establish what a good price to performance ratio is, then compare new offerings to the current “best case” scenario. That way if I can get the latest and greatest, I know what it is comparable to, regardless of personal opinions on how “new” or non “meh” the new offering is.

For example, let’s pretend the 5070 cards had no issues and really were comparable to the 4070, then would being able to get a 5070 up to a certain price be worth it? Etc….

Paramedic here. Assuming that you're reading the ECG with the "Pulse" logo right-side up, that ECG reading is showing bunny ears on the QRS complex, so straight off the bat, we're dealing with a Right Bundle Branch Block (RBBB), which is an impaired electrical conduction on the right side of the heart (assuming it's lead V1, of course).

We're also not seeing any T-waves after the QRS complex, so we also seem to be dealing with possible hypokalemia (a potassium deficiency). This can inhibit the depolarization of skeletal muscles, while making heart muscle cells excessively prone to depolarizing. The latter is particulary important, as excessive depolarization of the heart can lead to *cardiac arrest* in the form of pulseless ventricular tachycardia (pVT) or ventricular fibrillation (Vfib). The common causes of hypokalemia in the body are excessive excretion of blood potassium in the form of urine production, or a hormone imbalance (mainly high insulin and catecholamine levels).

Not to mention, the QRS itself is looking massively wide, so the impulses are likely being generated at the Purkinje Fibers instead of the SA or AV nodes. If that pulse rate gets faster than 40, the heart's likelihood of going into a pVT or a Vfib is pretty significant.

So yeah, that ECG isn't looking good. You're gonna have to start doing CPR and get that AED hooked up soon.

I would like to add a clarification at 4:25. This is the block diagram of GB202, the die used in the 5090. It has a total of 192 SMs, which is 96 TPCs, which are arranged into 12 GPCs of 8 TPCs each.

GB203, the die used in the 5080 and 5070ti, has a different layout inside. It has 84 SMs, which is 42 TPCs. These are arranged into 7 GPCs with 6 TPCs each. You can see this in die shots of each chip, with GB203 having 6 symmetric GPCs surrounding a central offset one that wedges its top TPC between the memory controllers on one long edge.

Presumably on this die, each group of 8 ROPs should be linked to 3 TPCs instead of 4 as in GB202. This makes it possibly a bit easier to mess it up on GB203, but it would somehow indicate that the 5080 here may only have 106 SMs working completely correctly.

Just as a little aside, in FFXIV there is a benefit in having your FPS go above you display refresh rate, if minuscule: your actions and skill queue time is tied to rendered frame, so playing at 30FPS vs playing at 120FPS can drastically change your experience. This is further exacerbated by your ping to their servers. In other words, playing with 120FPS allows you to i.e. dodge ground target AOEs that 30FPS doesn't allow you to. Same for skill queuing. Global cooldown time for skills / casts in this game is set at 2.5s, bar some exceptions. At 30FPS, you are disproportionately more likely to be clipping (i.e. losing uptime, the number of potential GCDs you can do in the e.g. 1 minute time window) when you try to weave 2 oGCD (Off-Global CoolDown) skills between GCD (Global CoolDown) compared to 120FPS, just because of the specific way the game is implemented and handles inputs, action queue and such. You throw in a random lag spike on your or their end and this can be really impactful. That's all folks.

But I would be really interested in seeing some empirical tests of how, if at all, does framegen impact input lag, just by the virtue of having more frames. Are the games sampling inputs more often thanks to the fake frames? Are they inconsequential? I would love to know.

In 5090, after the connector, all 12+ conductors are merged into one. What if, instead of a regular 12V-2X6 cable with separated 12+ phases into smaller wires, we use a single cable where all 12+ phases are combined into one thick conductor? If the current flows differently for each user depending on the resistance of the conductors, then there isn’t a specific current distribution scheme across the wire’s phases. In one video, some phases were even cut off, and the remaining ones took over the load. The main issue, however, is the wire heating due to the thin phase wires.

Tariffs raise the import cost on the base product. They do NOT raise a £2000 GPU by 10 or 25%- That is price gouging by sellers claiming tariffs raised prices. As a customs auditor I will explain how a 10% tariff will effect the price of a product vs how the merchant passes that on to you to gouge.

 A 10 % tariff on a container of RTX5090 would see the shipment accrue a tariff on the base value of the goods (value added tax in the UK and EU.)
 A base value of a single RTX5090 ships in at £700. The 10% tariff would see the GPU adjusted to a value of £770.

 Then the domestic shipper, distribution centre and resell merchant adds their profit on top of the product. 
 The price is adjusted for profits concerning add-in board partners. 

 Domestic merchants will effectively raise the shelf price by 10-25% , not the MUCH lower value added tax (tariff) charged at customs. 

 The best example is Nvidia punches the price through the roof for the AIB partners leaving them little room for profit but gives them maximum responsibility for the product. The goods are shipped and put on shelves, all in costing £900-£1100 per GPU and the gouging begins. The GPU is sold to the reseller  at an adjusted rate (£1100-£1300 per GPU) then says the £70 tariff is £300-£500 and passes on the price gouge to the consumer.

 An already massively over priced GPU at £2000 becomes £2500. The reality is a £2000 GPU adjusted for a 10% tariff would be £2,070-£2,140. The additional £300-£500 is strictly being tacked on an F YOU to consumers. Retailers will always cash in. It is business. 

 Nvidia uses the low tariff to mark their product price up, the AIB adds it in again, the merchant adds it in again. You are being triple charged at triple the rise when in reality the tariff only raises the price of the base card. 

 I feel like I wrote this out poorly. 

 The reason for the tariff is not to gouge the consumer, it is to force businesses to stop producing goods overseas, bring them back to that country where the product can be made at better prices. The production on home land would bring jobs and value to the economy. 

 Nvidia is not recouping money invested in tech (the government , tax payers,  investors have given them billions to cover that) they are simply gouging because they can and you are buying. 

 tl:dr you are charged the original producers and subsequent producer and seller all charge 3 times the amount of a tariff and triple charge you the actual cost, you actually pay for it and it continues to be a valid business practice.

Instrument Technician here. Hopefully I can help you guys with some terminology and understanding:
I have never used a machine like this, but many of the components seen here are related to my trade. For your measurements, Ps and dP, we would say "static pressure" and "differential pressure". Static pressure is the pressure on a medium, and differential pressure is the difference between two mediums. In this case, they are using differential pressure to measure a flowrate, which is common in many industrial industries. Flowrate is measured in those particular instances by measuring the pressure upstream and downstream of a precise, fixed sized orifice plate. When you move a gas through a fixed sized orifice plate, you end up with a repeatable, precise pressure drop, dependant of course upon a number of other variables. In the machine you are using, temperature is a critical variable, as is relative humidity. I suspect those holes you see in the middle of that chamber are different size orifice plates - which are used to accomodate the range of flowrates you desire to measure from the pressure drop on the downstream side.
Hope this helps!

As an engineer with some background into compressible fluid mechanics, I think the best way to present your testing is to completely segregate the fan testing from any other impedance testing like the front panel mesh. Since the fan testing machine can isolate for flow rate with the built in fan, test the pressure drop for impedance testing at different flow rates. Generate PV charts (pressure vs volume flow rate for the full range of fan speeds) for different fans to directly compare fans to each other (maybe include sound levels on the chart?). Then you can use the fan PV data and the impedance testing data to determine the performance of each fan for the given impedance. This way you can have a database to characterize all of the fans performance and get immediate results for each new impedance testing configuration and vis-versa (in college we used a program called Matlab to do these sort of calculations).

For charting the comparison between fans, you obviously cannot just overlay full PV fan curves as it will get way to cluttered, so I would focus on a PV chart overlaying the max RPM for each fan, and a separate PV chart for a noise normalized fan speed. For reporting on a front panel or some other impedance test, you could chart the flow rate produced by each of the fans at max RPM and the noise normalized speed which can be calculated from your baseline fan PV charts and impedance testing data.

Some other suggestions or things to note:
- I expect most of your audience have no idea how much a mmH2O or mmHg is, so maybe use different units for pressure.
- The noise and noise profile of a fan may change under load, you could report fan noise as a function of static pressure in your hemi-anechoic sound chamber (drink) with calibrated orifice plates mounted behind the fan.
- I highly recommend a software like Matlab to crunch all of the data, this could help your other day-to-day data analysis as well, I just looked and you can get a free trial on their website. 
- When testing for impedance, standardize the area of the mesh used to make the results directly comparable (you effectively did in this video, but it should be standardized (maybe a 120x120 or 140x140mm square?)

TLDR: Test fans and front panels independently, use data from those tests and the hemi-anechoic sound chamber to calculate meaningful data and make readable charts for individual fan or case reviews.

I'm not sure if measuring the FPS of a game tells the whole story. The PCIe bandwidth mainly affects things like how long it takes to stream in textures and other data onto the GPU. Most modern games do this asynchronously, so lower bandwidth there wouldn't really affect the FPS, but instead might have the game temporarily render with lower resolution textures as you move around the in-game world if the higher resolutions are struggling to load in time. PCIe connection can become a bottleneck with faster SSD, considering the data usually needs to get decompressed before it can be uploaded to the GPU.

Liquid metal used in thermal interfaces like this is most famous for not quite corrosion, but for things like penetrating other metal's crystal lattices and causing embrittlement. Galinstan alloys (of which most liquid metal cooling solutions consist of as far as I am aware) and aluminum is the most common example, where if the oxide layer of the aluminum is scratched off and the galinstan is allowed to make contact with the bare aluminum, it is soaked up like a sponge and the aluminum turns as brittle as a potato chip.

The noise spikes are very likely due to what is known as blade pass frequency (BPF). It's the fan rpm x no. of blades divide by 60. So for 7 blades @ ~1580rpm that gives 7 x 1580 / 60 = 184Hz. You will then see smaller spikes at harmonics of this, so 184x2=368Hz , 184x3=552 ...x4, x5, etc. We sometimes use this at work to indirectly measure a fans rpm just by looking at the sound profile with a spectrum analyser. 0:45 the 1080p bind may be a matter of "round trip time" between CPU and GPU at this point. Every draw call causes some communication between CPU and GPU that locks the CPU thread for a moment. So the total "GPU time" per frame is basically [task complexity]/[GPU speed) + [round trip time]. As the GPU speed increases towards absurd amounts, the total GPU-time asymptotically approaches the round trip time.

I think I have a way to explain how schlieren photography works.

When light passes through different mediums, say from air to water, it will slow down. if the light is entering at an angle, the speed change will cause the angle to also change. 

At certain angles light can bounce completely on the boundary between 2 mediums because of the difference in their densities. This is total internal reflection. At shallow angles, light will bounce off the boundary, but if the angle get steep enough, light will pass through the boundary. This is called the critical angle.

What schlieren photography is doing is taking advantage of the different densities of either the way air flows, or how it expands due to temperature Causing the light to either bounce go into the camera or away from it, causing a difference in brightness. This is what allows us to see the movement of the air.

Basically he's shining a light/laser of a specific wavelength that will show the distortions of air from the heat generated by the GPU.

Warmer air expands and cooler air contracts, that causes pressure difference in the air that also "visually" warps the air, but the camera setup and light he uses makes it easier to visualize the warps and wefts of air and heat,

BTF 3.0 sounds like a good idea in theory. It would be nice to have all the power inputs grouped into one spot on the motherboard. And having PCIe delivery through it would also be so much cleaner. However, sliding the PSU directly onto the board is going to destroy most existing case designs, and also open up issues where if the power delivery contacts are damaged, the entire motherboard is screwed. I think a good middle ground is to allow for 1 large modular flexible ribbon cable to handle all power delivery from the PSU to the motherboard (like the old IDE hard drive cable). This would allow existing cases to be forward-compatible, and make it less likely for motherboards to be accidentally damaged.

Those spl spikes are obviously related to the room, not the fan noise itself. They're called "room modes", basically the nodes where reflected sound waves (of the specific frequency) intersect either in phase or out of phase.

In-phase modes are constructive (spl spikes) and out of phase modes are destructive (spl dips).

Low frequencies are notoriously difficult to treat in a room as the physical wave lenghts are so damn long, and thus the sound absorbing material has to be really deep/thick. On the lower end of the low frequencies we're talking about several meters/yards deep/thick.

The remarkable thing is that an error of 1mm and an angle of 1° is enough to annihilate both the cpu and the motherboard. In the olden days the pins were further apart than that, and you could feel the cpu pins drop into the holes. If it went in level and you weren't heavy handed everything was good.  

The modern pins and pads are so delicate by comparison and there's no natural alignment within their mechanism.  Even tiny hand movements could damage the pins.  The design with alternating power and ground pins rather adds to the short circuit risk. Exciting.  Obviously there are the outer alignment notches, but clearly they are not fail safe. 

A better idea would be longer solid alignment pins (or notches) that have to aligned and engaged with before the final lowering of the cpu. Then the cpu would be aligned mechanically before even meeting the  tiny pins and well before the clamps are even touched. Reducing any alignment error below the critical level, which is probably only 1/4 of a pad, maybe less.

I made PCBs for a number of years and used the AOI (Automated Optical Inspection) machines that you spoke of. When you speculated that the AOI missed the alignment of the socket on the board, I laughed and immediately thought that there's no way. The system can and does detect the smallest deviations and will immediately flag them for review by the person at the end of the line. If for some reason it didn't flag it for review, it wouldn't flag any others with the same defect for review either, which would have resulted in a whole batch of defective motherboards burning up on people.They are also usually tested in-house before shipping, so it would have malfunctioned at that time and not at the end-user as seen here. Not to say that escapes don't happen, but it would be extremely unlikely in this case.

My next thought was to inspect the alignment of the processor within the socket and inspect the contact area of the pins and the processor. The next thing I know, that's exactly what you're doing! With that said, based on the evidence presented, I agree with your conclusions. This was human error. A expensive mistake.

The reason the battery warning is so large is due to a well-intentioned new law in the US called Reese's law, which regulates any consumer products that uses coin cell batteries. It was named after a child that died after ingesting a 2032CR. It requires warnings to be affixed to the packaging, and the warning sizes required by law are absolutely enormous. The size of warnings are absolutely disproportionate to the actual risk, and yes, it also is required even for when the coin cell is not accessible.

Long story short, expect more of these oversized warnings in short order.

And thats important for a prebuild, if the putt in a 850Watt PSU and a RTX4090 starts a fire, then they have a liability. EE Student here: The yellowish substance you see surrounding the die is the underfill. It provides structural support to the C4 bump array bonding the die to the green substrate interposer. It is critical that the underfill chemistry is compatible with the bump material (various lead free, high-lead, eutectic, etc), and compatible with the thermal stress the connection will go under. It's just a different type of underfill vs what you're used to seeing, with a different chemistry. But as long as it meets all the required constraints then it will be fine. Fun fact, failure to choose a proper underfill type is what caused the Xbox 360 RROD, PS3 YLOD, and notebook GPU failures a nearly 15 years ago.

Alta D1 owner here - Just got this case and am mid-build with it (waiting on more storage to arrive). For niche high-end workstation builds this thing is genuinely amazing and very well built, but it should be noted that one of the two reviewers on amazon (hence the 3.5 star rating) noted that they got a case that somehow got through QC without some screwholes being tapped, and one screwhole being ruined from being tapped twice on the same part. Neither the other reviewer on amazon nor  I have encountered this problem so it was likely a rejected part (hence the untappped screwholes) that accidentally got put back onto the assembly line.

Cases designed around niche server or workstation usecases do tend to be rather expensive. If its not your niche, yeah its way overpriced - but if it IS your niche, its a dream case and something I would fully recommend. In my case though (pun not intended), I'm building an Epyc workstation with the enormous 13"x13" asrockrack GENOAD8X-2T and enough storage to actually make use of all that IO - but the build itself comes with a pricetag high enough that an $800 case that supports all the parts is actually quite sensible.

AI (LLM) Temperature tuning means that word choice is flexible, and it'll chose the option it has 10% confidence in over the option it has 40% confidence in *some* times. And this makes for better, more natural writing more often. But, picking "2020" when you're 10% sure (because, well, it's a year, and it's close to 2019) instead of "2018" which you're 80% sure (because that's what all but one sources agree is correct) is the kind of garbage only LLM summaries can be.

Getting different answers is a feature. It's an integral part of the model. The problem is it's totally willing to pick the 2nd or 3rds best "fact", even if it's very confident that the 1st best is correct. "close enough" is basically fine when you're describing the form and color of some background detail that you're not supposed to closely examine. It's usually better than just a blank wall. But "AI" designers and users need to learn the difference between important factual tokens that *should not* be high Temperature, and syntactic fluff that a synonym for is acceptable.

It’s wild how the Alder Lake CPUs, especially the 12900K, have managed to stay so relevant even as newer generations keep rolling in. Intel really hit a sweet spot back in 2021, balancing decent performance, new tech (DDR5, PCIe Gen 5), and reasonable prices. Even now, CPUs like the 12900K and 12700K are holding their ground, performing like modern i5s in a lot of cases. That’s a pretty good deal if you snagged one for $120 in a Best Buy clearance. 

What I love about Alder Lake is the flexibility! it works with DDR4 or DDR5, so you don’t need to throw your whole build into the trash if you want an upgrade. Plus, it shares a socket with the newer chips, which is rare these days. You can slap in a 14900K if you really want to push your system, though most people probably don’t need that kind of power (or heat).

One thing to consider about 12th Gen is it is now really the only option for ITX builds at the moment (excluding 13, 14th for obvious issues and heat and 200 series for price to performance).  Am5 boards are fewer in number, more expensive (in Europe at least) and limited io compared to their 1700 counterparts. The amount of AM5 itx boards with only 1 graphics port on the rear io is ridiculous!  Considering ITX is the only form factor where you are most likely need to use the IGPU if you need to use the PCI slot for something other than a graphics card.

I think some perspective is sorely needed here. Raptor Lake's microcode issue is a red herring muddying the waters. 13th Gen is undeniably a better architecture than Alder Lake, the same way 14th is better than 13th. While clock-for-clock IPC on the P-cores is a dead heat, each successive gen is more power efficient, significantly so when you compare RL-Refresh to Alder Lake. The microcode issues were often BIOS and chipset-dependent (B- and H-series chipsets mostly immunized your CPU because if their inherent voltage bondage-and-discipline). What I'm getting at is that the microcode issues are an arbitrary side-show that has nothing to do with the fundamental architecture; Alder Lake could have easily been affected in the same way had the stars aligned differently, if you follow me. 

A B760 owner who's CPU never received voltage spikes objectively had a better system than the equivalent Alder Lake. They didn't have a _worse_ system than Alder lake simply because _somebody else's_ bleeding-edge Z790 was zapping the CPU, did they? Of course not.

Just to the discussion of the hemi-anechoic chamber: Any chance you guys can do noise testing for PSU's that you test? I've had multiple PSU's that have been unusually loud, often louder than the other components in my system at idle, even from noise focused brands like be quiet!. For my latest PSU from be quiet!, I found that the noise was coming from a resonance in the heat sinks on the mosfets, and the fan controller power delivery producing a pulsing sound from the fan. 

My solution, which I did "AT MY OWN RISK!", was a single rubber grommet wedged in each heat sink to dampen the resonance, and replacing the fan with a be quiet! PWM fan controlled from the mobo, and running a custom fan curve.

As for anyone wondering why Micro Center has exclusivity on these...
The 7000 series of processors has two major chips in them. The IO controller and one or two CCD. These are the same in all of the processors only they differ in the number of cores they have.

All cores are located on the CCD, or  Core Complex Die, and one CCD has eight (8) cores in total. This means that a 7600 only have one CCD and only six of these are activated. Now the CCD in a 7600 can be complete but with two disabled cores or it might have one or two damaged cores that's been deactivated. Meanwhile the 7700, 7800 and 8700 processors also has one CCD, but it's working completely with all eight cores. That means that both the 7600, 7700 and 7800 cost the same to manufacture. The 7900 has a total of twelve cores, so two CCD with six active cores on each while the 7950 also have two CCD but with all eight cores active on each for a total of 16 cores. Now we get to the 7800X3D. This has one full CCD or eight cores. Meanwhile the 7600X3d only have six cores on the CCD. Again the manufacturing cost for these processors is the same, but one has to be sold cheaper. To make this economical AMD are only building 7600X3D with CCD that is damaged so they can only use six cores. when building a 7600 they can afford to use full CCD and disable cores when they have to but the 7600X3D has an extra chiplet with the 3D cache. This makes them more expensive to make so AMD want to sell as many 7800X3D as possible, and with the market chowing down on these they have had no problem of selling them. Now the manufacturing yield has improved over time and those CCD are not all that common and they can't make enough 7600X3D to meet demands from the entire market, and yet they have a trickle of suitable CCD. Either they would be sitting on a small set of processors in stock or they sell what they got. Selling to the entire market would make them very had to keep in stock, so they looked at the market and chose to sell all of them to one reseller, Micro Center. Now you can buy them from Micro Center but even then they can tend to sell out as they are pretty cheap, and as shown here often outperforms 7700X3D in games even though that processor is more expensive.

Looking back, that got to be a long explanation.

Short explanation: The limited access to damaged CCD (core Complex Die) with six working cores makes it uneconomical to make 7600X3D processors with full CCD and disable two cores. So the limited supply is sold to Micro Center. Spreading it over the entire market would make it very hard to come by as so few are available.

Just for some relevant info here: my motherboard died which force me to Microcenter for a replacement. Instead of just getting another motherboard for my 14700k, I picked up this Core Ultra 7 265k and a gigabyte Z890 - with the MC card and in-store deal, it was $450 after tax.
In every benchmark I have run, the 265k has outscored the 14700k. With a 4090, I game at 4k and, again, I seem to have a better experience now than with the 14700k along with alot less heat. I had a 360 AIO cooler to keep the 14700k in check but it seems overkill now with the 265k (which I rarely see ever go north of 55C). Also noticed my 4090 now at the full PCIE4 at x16 - I hadn't factored that in before, but the 265k offers 24 lanes to the 14700k's 20 and since I have 2 NVME drives installed, with the 14700k it was bumping the 4090 down to PCIE4x8 (not really a problem because that is still equivalent to PCIE3x16). Still, having the 4090 at the full x16 instead of x8 was a sort of "bonus". Overall, my experience with the 265k, I would say, has been very good. I do alot of CAD and rendering as well as gaming and in all aspects, it's delivered.
I should note that this is as of April and not only has the pricing come down significantly on this chip, but also there have been a number of BIOS updates (all seemingly addressing performance) and so my experience with the chip is in an environment that see the chip both cheaper and operating on a more mature platform than Steve's testing at the time. Maybe that makes a difference, maybe not.
IMO if you use your PC for more than just gaming and if you aren't gaming at 1080p, then this isn't a bad way to go. In my use cases, it's been a great CPU so far and I have a better opinion of it than my old 14700k.
I don't have Steve's knowledge and test equipment, but in my own experiences, this 265k overall feels like a better CPU than my old 14700k.

Much as I appreciate having simulation games like stellaris and/or factorio in the benchmarks, I think you may be running a bit too small of a save file for those. As you increase the load to the point that people would actually start having issues, the relative scaling tends to shift a lot. 

Ex- factorio is a game that is locked to 60 UPS, so looking at a save that has CPUs giving 200-400 UPS means little since they are all more then fine, while a save which is pushing top end CPUs down to around 60 UPS really shows which CPUs will actually make a difference in terms of how large the factory can grow before you get issues. And logic may expect that a CPU giving 400 UPS vs one giving 300 will mean that at 60, it becomes 60 vs 45, but it winds up performing differently, given that as the base gets bigger, the importance of memory speed, latency, cache, and cpu speed change a lot. I expect something similar to hold true in stellaris. 

Overall, my thought here is that you may get better results looking not for how the CPUs compare when running the game normally, but rather at how far they let you get with the game before performance drops below acceptable levels. I have been kicking around several ideas for potentially good benchmarks in this vein, looking into the point that the CPU actually starts to degrade the experience for the user, since most of the data currently posted, while useful for relative comparisons, doesn't really show how things wind up looking at that cliff, for the things where you actually can hit that cliff.

I work as an electrician in germany. I mostly saw this kind of failure in outlets which were used to their maximum capacity at regular intervals. They used normal 230V sockets which are rated for 16A for their forklift chargers. What they didnt know was, that these plugs were actually rated for 10A continuous operation. At first nothing will happen. But everyday the socket was overloaded and got warm during operation. When it cooled down again a little bit of condensation formed inside the connector and the resistance got a little bit higher. This cycle continued for while until the socket failed completely and caught on fire.

So the actual failure was not that the connector was bad, but it got overloaded everyday and the cycle between cold and warm increased the resistance until the failure accured.

I could also imagine that this factor can also come into play with the 12VHPWR. 
But I cant understand why they would put such a high load on such a small connector. And the fact that you have to be extra careful to not stress the pins while installing these is a huge design oversight. Just look at an XT60/90 connector and how easy it is to connect those.

Would be nice if they would build some kind of failsafe into the connector such as a PTC thermistor. If that would be implemented in the future you could give the user a message that the connection is bad before the connector melts and shut down the card into a low Power mode.

As a hobbyist electronics guy that has built some PSU adapter cables and such for people, I decided to look into the difference between 12VHPWR and PCIe power connectors at a component level.

PCIe 6-pin and 8-pin connectors, as well as ATX power supplies, the extra 4-pin ATX12V board connectors, etc. use Molex Mini-Fit Jr. pins. I got to looking in to what pins are used for 12VHPWR, and someone pointed out that it's Amphenol Minitek PWR 3.0, plus listed some part numbers, so I got to digging.

Looking at the drawings for female pins from each family rated for 16AWG wire, the MiniTek PWR 3.0 pins are smaller in the outside dimensions of the folded-rectangle shape of the female pins, and the pin contact length is shorter than the roughly-equivalent Mini-Fit Jr. female pins used for PCIe and other connectors. Oddly enough, the Amphenol docs list their pins being capable of up to 12.0A per circuit, while Molex lists theirs as up to 9.0A per circuit. I'm sure if I really wanted to dig and do some math, I could come up with the total contact area between the female receptacle and male pin for each family as well, but I think the point is clear by now. The MiniTek PWR 3.0 pins are going to have a smaller contact surface area between the male and female pin than the Mini-Fit Jr. pins even when engaged properly, yet the MiniTek PWR 3.0 pins are rated for a third *more* current than the Mini-Fit Jr. Pins.

Since each pin in the 12VHPWR connector is rated for 9.5A by the PCI-SIG spec, that gives you a total supported power of 684W...In a perfect world. That gives you a 14% safety margin, again in a perfect world. Let's say that one of these six pins drops out due to a poor connection...Then you've got 600W running over five pins. 5*9.5A*12V is 570W, but you're trying to push 600W over those five pins...Congrats, you just put yourself at high risk of thermal runaway.

The safety margin isn't there with the Amphenol pins. IMHO, it would be safer to run a 6x2 Molex Mini-fit Jr arrangement technically out-of-spec than the 6x2 Amphenol MiniTek PWR 3.0 arrangement technically within spec in an improperly-installed plug/receptacle, simply due to the larger contact area with the Mini-Fit Jr. pins. Physics doesn't lie; the lower safety margin of the Amphenol setup puts the designer behind the eight ball right off the hop, then you add a connector that doesn't positively latch? No wonder these things are melting. This was a bad design choice on NVIDIA's part. NVIDIA is 100% counting on a perfect engagement every time between those twelve pins, and even one pin being off puts you out-of-spec according to the PCI-SIG spec. Once the first pin heats up, its resistance goes up...Which is going to drive more current to the lower-resistance pins, causing them to be over-spec even more and heat up as well.

If they started making interconnects using flexible 20sqmm or so (4awg) cable and used a larger more beefy connector, literally none of these issues would ever exist.

One quibble, though: when multiple pins share the current at the connector block, but the 0 and 12 V groups are shorted together on either side of the connector, it's *not* the high resistance pins which will get hot, but the **LOW** resistance pins which are of course carrying the most current. This is because the power dissipated in each pin is V*I, and since the voltage drop across the pins is forced to be identical (...as I say, shorted on either side) the pins carrying more current are the ones which will melt.
Add a bunch of resistance to 5 of the 6 12 V pins, for example, and it's the final one which will melt when you pass 50 A through the connector.

I have a background (degree) in computer engineering and I very much enjoyed my class specifically on optics and how to design cables.... Great topic.

Now, as a design engineer your task is to understand the spec, design the product to meet the spec, and to work with certification to verify performance. 

If we want to take a step back I can give you 4-5 main things I would investigate or inquire further for why this happened. This is a broader term.... Computer design engineering puzzle.... And I think many people failed to do their jobs along the way. 

1. Molex failed to design connectors and cables that were able to operate correctly. They had to be redesigned and my instincts tell me that they will have to be revised again.

2. ATX, PCI-E, Nvidia, and Intel all failed to verify the spec appropriately.  Specs are designed to be upgraded, improved. However, you should be able to have a standard that works the vast majority of the time and the reason specs exist is to have a reliable product in manufacturing.  This is because of engineering calculations needing to have a reliable tolerance. However you want to cut it, the spec(s) are not reliable and need to be revised..... Again. 

(Sidenote: imagine if this was ANSI and it was a screw on the space shuttle.... Netflix has great documentaries about this)

3. Manufacturers had the issue of demand from the designers of the products (Nvidia, Corsair, Asus, etc.) which led to extremely terrible quality control due to a variety of factors. The common mantra is "ship it and we'll figure it out later" because the timeline of sales matters way more to the business mindset than the certification and engineering concerns. Think about profit margin vs. replacement costs. Often you will see inferior products added onto quality designs due to availability because at that specific moment the product was already manufactured and engineering is told to update their design to allow it. Certification is told they have to accept it through simple analysis. And this is what leads to Boeing having their massive issues with the dreamliner.

4.  No one considered the basic functionality of the product and NOBODY did long term testing for fatigue failures. Things were done in such a brief timeline that it was not possible to test them thoroughly, which is more clear when you step back and think about why this all happened. 

5. No one really cared or understood what bend radius means in the design requirements sense. You can even see this from the actual pictures in the spec. 

Computer cases have been designed in such a way for how long? No one thought it was a good idea to run every single design constraint on this cable+connector on an open bench scenario where there aren't things jammed into some small enclosure. The stack up of massive connector on the card into massive connector on the cable into computer literally does not work with bend radius (cable) design guidelines.  Talk to a person who works with sheet metal and ask them about bend radius and why it matters. Ask them about different types of metal and how the bend requirements change based on the material itself that you're using. Now.... Consider that the vast majority of phone cables fail because the weight of the wire itself and the relatively small size of the connector.  Flip that on its head.... Now you have a massive connector trying to jam itself into a small space. It doesn't work when you need (in both situations) proper bend radius to prevent signal and connector failures.

How we fix this as a whole......
A. You need a minimum clearance and bend radius guideline for CASE MANUFACTURERS.
B. You need power supply manufacturers to meet a specific quality standard for clean power signals and standardization of what the cables need to do (this is from ATX spec)
C. You need motherboards, video cards, and OEMs to follow the actual specs and not mess things up by trying to push limits (waves at Nvidia)
D. You need to design things in such a way that they aren't designed to fail. 

Step back and think about 6-pin and 8-pin connectors. You have a clip and it's attached on one side to keep a power cable from disconnecting and sparking on the board or somewhere else. 

Now, you have 2x6 or 2x8 connectors, even 24-pin connectors which have been used for a long time to send signals and various power connections from the PSU to the board reliably for years, decades.  All of those connectors were not this big and didn't require this much power.  It's a massive tolerance issue and the entire thing is centered around this very cheap clip that supposedly going to magically hold down this massive duct-taped connector design to the card while being jammed into place because the computer door won't shut and the weight of everything alone is too heavy to keep it in place. 

You should have 2-4 clips. Not just one. 

Fix the spec... Fix the connector.... Fix the quality issues..... Then maaaaaybe it'll be reliable.

The wood likely split because of the metal backing plate, not despite it. Metal and wood expand and contract at different rates and for different reasons (metal: temperature, wood: humidity). 

Fully adhering metal to wood in this fashion will run such a risk, especially if the production process doesn't monitor the wood moisture levels, or if any part of the processing after the wood and metal are affixed has extreme temperatures or humidity levels. That includes shipping.

Looking at that split, what likely happened  was just a localized moist spot in the wood when it was adhered to the metal. Then as the wood shrank as water dissipated and normalized, the metal held it in place when it was slightly expanded like a sponge. The "crack" is a split along the grain in an obvious weak spot.

The metal would help protect against impacts, flexing, etc. But the glue or even the metal itself isn't strong enough to keep wood from expanding or contracting with water/humidity.

If the fastening of a wooden part to a rigid, non-organic material does not have room for wood movement it will be the chief cause of cracking/splitting. The wood will want to expand  and contract but it will not have the room or flexibility to do so. Are the holes used to fasten the wood to the metal ovals (instead of circles) that are also perpendicular to the grain direction?

If it's some kind of adhesive, it should be the kind that has high 'gumminess' after curing to maybe let the wood move on its own a bit. That would be borderline but mostly fine.

But, I'm guessing what happened here happened because the wood is thin and fixed in-place at the same time. I would hazard a guess that a 20% thicker wood panel would have less of a chance of cracking. Since PC cases heat up and cool down regularly and rapidly, and the wood is fixed to what is a very thermally conductive and rigid material, I would prefer slightly thicker wood, and maybe mechanical fasteners that have room for movement.

Love to see you keep up the ITX case reviews! A note about the wood: it's pretty obvious that this would crack, if I'm understanding what they did right. It looks like they glued the entire wooden panel, or at least the outer edges, to the metal frame. This is a recipe for cracked wood, and is exactly the opposite of what you want to do to avoid cracking. Any solid piece of wood (as opposed to laminated, plywood, particle board, etc.) will expand and contract with humidity and temperature changes. This is entirely unavoidable, and the effects are especially noticeable on thinner panels, and I'd expect all the cutouts to just make this even more so. What they'd want to do to avoid cracking is to mount the wood loosely, in a way that doesn't restrict its movement more than what is necessary. This is how wooden tabletops are mounted, for example - with mounting mechanisms that allow for wood movement, as otherwise the tension from expansion and contraction will warp and crack it. I hope I'm wrong about how this is mounted, but if not, Fractal is going to have to replace *a lot* of these panels.
